checklist.step: Rebuild the register of collection trigger points
actions: Open the Privacy module and list every processing activity whose source field is 'collected from data subject' (Art. 13) or 'obtained from a third party' (Art. 14).

Ask each channel owner - Digital Channel Manager, Broker Relationship Manager, Claims Director / Manager, Marketing Manager - to confirm every screen, form, letter and call script that captures personal data for their channel.
Add one register row per trigger with: channel, screen or form name, system, data categories, purpose, lawful basis and the notice version that must fire.
Flag rows where the data arrives indirectly (broker submission, credit bureau pull, medical report, telematics provider) - those carry the 30-day Art. 14(3) clock.
checklist.done: every live collection point across EU and UK channels has a register row naming its system, purpose and required notice version.

checklist.step: Tie each trigger to its RoPA purpose and lawful basis
actions: Pull the Art. 30 record for each trigger and copy the declared purpose, Art. 6 basis and (where applicable) Art. 9(2) condition onto the register row.
Reject any trigger whose form captures a field not listed in the RoPA purpose - send it back to the channel owner as a data-minimisation defect before writing notice text around it.
Where the basis is Art. 6(1)(f) legitimate interests, attach the LIA reference so the notice can state the interest pursued as Art. 13(1)(d) demands.
Record the retention period per purpose so the notice can state it rather than saying 'as long as necessary'.
checklist.done: each trigger row carries a RoPA purpose, an Art. 6 basis, any Art. 9(2) condition, an LIA reference where relevant and a stated retention period.

checklist.step: Draft the Art. 13 layer for directly collected data
actions: Write the short-form layer that sits on the collection screen and the long-form notice behind it, covering every Art. 13(1)-(2) element: controller identity and contact, DPO contact, purposes and legal basis, legitimate interests pursued, recipients or categories of recipients, third-country transfers and the Art. 46 safeguard relied on, retention period, the data-subject rights, the right to withdraw consent, the right to lodge a complaint with a supervisory authority, whether provision is statutory or contractual and the consequence of not providing, and the existence of automated decision-making with meaningful information about the logic.
Name the actual recipient categories an insurer uses - reinsurers, loss adjusters, medical examiners, anti-fraud databases, claims service providers - not 'our partners'.
State the Irish DPC and the ICO by name as the complaint routes for EU and UK subjects respectively.
Send the draft to the Data Protection Officer for the Art. 39(1)(a) advice note and file the reply.
checklist.done: a drafted Art. 13 notice text exists in which every mandatory element is present and traceable to the register row it serves.

checklist.step: Draft the Art. 14 layer for data obtained from other sources
actions: Extend the notice with the two elements Art. 14 adds: the categories of personal data obtained and the source of the data, including whether it came from a publicly accessible source.

Name the real sources used in underwriting and claims - the broker or agent, the credit reference agency, the DVLA/claims-history database, the treating physician or medical reporting agency, the telematics device provider.

Add the Art. 14(5) exemption analysis for any source where notice is claimed to be impossible or disproportionate, with the reasoning written out and dated - never leave a source unnotified without one.
Have the Data Protection Officer counter-sign any Art. 14(5) exemption claim before it is relied on.
checklist.done: the Art. 14 layer names every indirect source and data category, and any exemption claim is written out and counter-signed by the DPO.

checklist.step: Write the rights block covering restriction, objection and profiling
actions: Set out each right separately with how to exercise it: access (Art. 15), rectification (Art. 16), erasure (Art. 17), restriction (Art. 18), portability (Art. 20), objection (Art. 21) and the Art. 22 automated-decision right.
Present the Art. 21(2) right to object to direct marketing explicitly and separately from the other rights, as Art. 21(4) requires, at the point of first communication.
Explain in plain words what restriction under Art. 18 means for an open claim - the file is held but not further processed except for legal claims.
State the one-month Art. 12(3) response time and the DSAR intake route so the notice and the DSAR procedure say the same thing.
checklist.done: the notice states each right, its exercise route, the one-month response time, and presents the direct-marketing objection right separately.

checklist.step: Add the special-category and criminal-conviction paragraph
actions: Identify from the RoPA every trigger that captures health, biometric or genetic data (medical evidence in underwriting and claims) or Art. 10 conviction data (motor and fraud screening).

State the Art. 9(2) condition relied on - explicit consent under Art. 9(2)(a), establishment or defence of legal claims under Art. 9(2)(f), or substantial public interest under Art. 9(2)(g) with the member-state law that provides it.
For Art. 10 data, cite the domestic law authorising the processing rather than asserting a bare legitimate interest.
Where explicit consent is the condition, make the consent statement a separate affirmative action on the form and not part of the terms acceptance.
checklist.done: every special-category and conviction-data trigger has a named Art. 9(2) condition or domestic legal authority stated in the notice.

checklist.step: Localise, translate and readability-check each notice version
actions: Produce the notice in every language a covered market sells in, and record the translation vendor and date for each.
Run a plain-language pass so the text meets Art. 12(1) 'concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible, using clear and plain language'.
Produce the child-facing wording for any journey that can enrol a minor, per Art. 12(1) last sentence.
Send translated versions back to Privacy Counsel for a back-translation check of the rights and legal-basis paragraphs before publication.
checklist.done: every market has an approved, plain-language notice version with the translation source and date recorded.

checklist.step: Wire the notice into the direct digital journeys
actions: Place the short-form notice above the first personal-data field on the quote and application screens, with the full notice one click away and reachable without login.
Configure the page to record notice version id, timestamp and the subject identifier when the screen is served - not when the form is submitted.
Confirm the notice is served before any cookie or tag that profiles the visitor fires, and that consent-dependent tags stay blocked until an affirmative action.
Raise a change request to remove any pre-ticked box or bundled consent found on the journey and retest after release.
checklist.done: every digital collection screen serves the current notice before the first field and writes a versioned, timestamped delivery record.

checklist.step: Wire the notice into the broker and agent intake path
actions: Attach the current notice to the quote and bind confirmation packs the portal generates, so the notice travels with the submission.
Add a portal field where the broker records the date the notice was given to the applicant, and make it mandatory before submission.
Update the intermediary agreement pack with the requirement to hand the insurer notice at collection and to send the insurer the date it was given.
For submissions where the broker did not deliver a notice, route the record to the Art. 14 30-day queue so the insurer issues it directly.
checklist.done: every broker submission carries either a broker-delivered notice date or an entry in the Art. 14 30-day issue queue.

checklist.step: Wire notices into FNOL and third-party claimant contact
actions: Add the privacy notice to the FNOL acknowledgement letter and email template so it goes out on first contact with the claimant.

Create a separate third-party claimant notice covering Art. 14 - what data was received from the policyholder, the anti-fraud database checks, and the legal-claims basis - and attach it to the first outbound letter to that claimant.
Add the notice to the medical-authorisation pack sent before any treating-physician report is requested.
Set the correspondence template to stamp the notice version and send date onto the claim file activity history.
checklist.done: FNOL, third-party claimant and medical-authorisation correspondence all carry a version-stamped notice recorded on the claim file.

checklist.step: Wire notices and preference capture into marketing collection
actions: Attach the marketing notice to every landing page, lead form and event capture, and block form publication without a linked notice id.
Record consent evidence per Art. 7(1): who consented, when, to what wording, by what action, and the notice version shown.
Put the Art. 21(2) objection route (unsubscribe plus a standing preference centre) in every outbound message header and footer.
Suppress any list segment whose records have no notice id or no consent evidence until it is remediated.
checklist.done: no marketing capture form or send list is live without a linked notice version and per-record consent evidence.

checklist.step: Run the 30-day clock for indirectly obtained data
actions: Schedule a daily job that reads new records from the indirect-acquisition feeds - broker submissions, bureau pulls, medical reporting agency returns, telematics enrolments - and writes an Art. 14 notice-due row with acquisition date plus 30 days.
Suppress rows where the subject has already been sent the current notice version through another channel, and log the suppression reason.
Trigger the outbound notice through the correspondence template and write the send timestamp back onto the row.
Escalate any row still open at day 27 to the Privacy Officer by email with the record identifiers listed.
checklist.done: every indirectly obtained record has a notice-due row that is closed by a timestamped send, a logged suppression, or an escalation before day 30.

checklist.step: Version, publish and archive the notice estate
actions: Publish each approved notice as a locked PDF named <channel>-<jurisdiction>-<version>-<effective date> and record its effective-from date.
Set the superseded version's withdrawn date on the same day the replacement goes live so no gap or overlap exists in the history.
Apply the 7-years-after-policy-or-claim-closure retention label to every version.
Confirm the repository index makes versions retrievable by channel, jurisdiction and date-in-force, which is how a regulator will ask for them.
checklist.done: the notice history is gapless, each version has effective and withdrawn dates, and versions are retrievable by channel, jurisdiction and date.

checklist.step: Capture per-record proof of delivery
actions: Confirm each channel writes a notice-delivery record holding subject id, channel, notice version id, delivery timestamp and delivery method.
Reconcile the daily count of delivery records against the daily count of new quotes, submissions, FNOLs and marketing captures, and investigate any channel with a shortfall the same week.
Fix silent failures at source - a channel that collects but writes no delivery record is treated as non-compliant until it does.
Produce a monthly delivery-coverage figure per channel for the DPO's report.
checklist.done: every collection event has a matching delivery record and monthly coverage is reported per channel.

checklist.step: Log notice exceptions and take DPO sign-off
actions: Raise an exception for every collection point running without a current notice, every Art. 14 send past 30 days and every unsupported Art. 14(5) exemption claim.
Assign root cause (new journey released without privacy review, template not updated, feed not wired to the 30-day job, broker non-delivery) and a named channel owner.
Decide and record whether a retrospective notice goes out and whether the incident meets the threshold for a supervisory-authority conversation.
Sign the remediation closure only when the retest evidence for that channel is attached.
checklist.done: every notice exception is logged with root cause, owner, retrospective-notice decision and a DPO-signed closure backed by retest evidence.

testing.step: Build the population of collection events for the quarter
actions: Extract every EU and UK collection event with a create date in the quarter: quotes and applications, broker submissions, bureau and medical report pulls, FNOL records, third-party claimant records and marketing form captures.
Stamp each row with channel, source (direct vs indirect), country of the data subject and the acquisition timestamp.
Add channels the register lists but the extract does not return - a channel with zero rows is a finding, not an empty set.
Sign the extract as complete and record the query, run date and row count in the workpaper.
testing.done: a signed, channel-complete population extract exists with source type and acquisition timestamp on every row.

testing.step: Reconcile the population to the systems of record
actions: Compare the quote and application count to the Policy Administration Platform new-business report for the same quarter and jurisdictions.
Compare the FNOL and third-party claimant counts to the Guidewire ClaimCenter claim-created report.
Compare marketing capture counts to the marketing automation platform form-submission report.
Investigate and document every variance over 1% before drawing the sample, and re-extract if the variance is unexplained.
testing.done: the population reconciles to policy, claims and marketing systems of record within 1%, with each variance explained in writing.

testing.step: Draw and document the sample
actions: Take 100% of the indirect-acquisition channels' notice-due rows that ran close to the 30-day limit (day 25 or later).
Take 40 records selected at random with a recorded seed, stratified so every live channel and both jurisdictions contribute at least 5 records.
Record population size, seed, strata and draw date so the sample can be re-created exactly.
Note any channel with too few records to stratify and test it 100% instead.
testing.done: a reproducible, channel-stratified sample of at least 40 records is documented with seed and strata.

testing.step: Re-perform the notice-content test against Art. 13 and Art. 14
actions: Build a grid with one column per Art. 13(1)-(2) and Art. 14(1)-(2) element and one row per notice version in the sample.
Read the notice version that was in force on each sampled record's acquisition date - not today's version - and tick each element only where the text actually states it.
Mark as a defect any element covered only by a generic phrase such as 'our partners' or 'as long as necessary' with no named recipients or stated period.
For indirect sources, confirm the data categories and the named source appear, and read any Art. 14(5) exemption claim against the actual facts.
testing.done: each in-force notice version has a completed element grid, with every missing or generic element recorded as a defect.

testing.step: Trace each sampled record to a timestamped delivery artifact
actions: Open the delivery record for each sampled subject and read notice version id, delivery timestamp, channel and method.
For claims records, open the ClaimCenter activity history and confirm the FNOL or claimant letter carrying the notice was actually despatched, not just generated.
For marketing records, open the consent evidence and confirm it names the wording version shown at capture.
Treat any record with no delivery artifact as a fail even where the channel is known to serve the notice on screen.
testing.done: every sampled record traces to a delivery artifact naming a version and a timestamp, or is recorded as a fail.

testing.step: Recompute the Art. 14(3) 30-day maths
actions: For every sampled indirect record, recompute elapsed days = notice send timestamp minus acquisition timestamp.
Compare against the 30-day limit and against the earlier trigger of first communication with the data subject, where such a communication happened first.
List every record over 30 days and every record where the insurer wrote to the subject before sending the notice.
Recompute the suppression logic on a sample of 10 suppressed rows and confirm the subject really had received the same in-force version.
testing.done: elapsed-day maths is recomputed for every sampled indirect record and each breach of the 30-day or first-communication trigger is listed.

testing.step: Re-walk the live collection journeys as a data subject
actions: Start a fresh quote in each live EU and UK journey and screen-capture the first screen that asks for personal data.
Confirm the notice appears above the first field, opens without login, and that the version served matches the current published version in the document management repository.
Check the browser network trace for profiling tags firing before an affirmative consent action, and record any that do.
Repeat the walk on the Broker & Agent Portal submission screen and on a marketing landing page, capturing each.
testing.done: every live journey has a dated screen capture showing the current notice served before first collection, with any early-firing tag recorded.

testing.step: Test version control across the notice estate
actions: Pull the full version history per channel and jurisdiction and plot effective-from and withdrawn dates on a timeline.
Flag any gap where no version was in force and any overlap where two versions claim the same day.
Confirm each published version carries a dated DPO approval and, for translated versions, a back-translation check record.
Confirm the 7-year retention label is applied to superseded versions and that none has been hard-deleted.
testing.done: the version timeline is gapless and overlap-free, each version has a dated DPO approval, and retention labels are intact.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one issue per exception recording channel, record identifiers, which Art. 13/14 element or deadline failed and the number of data subjects affected.
Assign root cause - journey released without privacy review, stale template, feed not wired to the 30-day job, broker non-delivery, translation not published - and a named owner.
Set a remediation date and, where the population affected is material, ask the Data Protection Officer to decide on a retrospective notice campaign.
Carry every open issue into the next quarter's test as a mandatory retest row.
testing.done: every exception has an issue with root cause, owner, affected-subject count, remediation date and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Compute the content-defect rate, the delivery-coverage rate and the count of Art. 14 sends past 30 days, and compare each to the stated thresholds.
Write the conclusion - effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective - citing the workpaper references behind each figure.
Have the Internal Auditor, who drafted and approved no sampled notice version, sign the workpaper as independent reviewer.

Report the conclusion and any open notice gaps to the Data Protection Officer and the Privacy Committee at its next sitting and file the workpaper under REG-020-C01 in the compliance evidence repository.
testing.done: a signed workpaper with a stated conclusion, the three computed rates and a dated committee reporting entry is filed in the evidence repository.

In-scope processes.value: Intake, identity verification, scoping, retrieval, redaction, response and closure for access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection and Art. 22 requests from policyholders, claimants, third-party claimants, brokers' clients, employees and candidates, in the EU and the UK

Compliance procedure documented.value: Data Subject Rights Procedure - published DPO contact routes, 24-hour intake logging, Art. 12(6) identity verification, scoping and search plan, exemption assessment, redaction and second review, response pack build, and the Art. 12(3) clock with its two-month extension test

Compliance procedure approved.value: Approved by the Data Protection Officer with Privacy Counsel; reviewed annually and after any EDPB right-of-access guidance update or upheld supervisory-authority complaint

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: Respond without undue delay and within one month of receipt (Art. 12(3)); where extended, the data subject must be told of the extension and the reasons within that same first month; erasure and rectification must also be communicated to recipients under Art. 19

Deadline reminders configured.value: Case SLA clock starts at receipt, not at identity verification; automated nudges to the case owner at day 7, day 14 and day 21, escalation to the DPO at day 25, and a mandatory extension-decision task at day 20

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: Every response issued after the deadline, every unlogged request found in a mailbox or call recording, and every unsupported refusal is logged as a privacy exception with root cause, owner and remediation date

Remediation sign-off captured.value: Counsel signs off every refusal, every exemption applied to withheld material and every late response before it is sent, and clears any complaint response to a supervisory authority

checklist.step: Publish and prove the DPO contact routes
actions: Publish the DPO contact - functional mailbox, postal address and the DSAR webform link - in every privacy notice, on the public website privacy page and in policy and claim correspondence footers.
Confirm the DPO's contact details are the ones notified to the lead supervisory authority under Art. 37(7) and update the DPC and ICO registrations if they have changed.
Send a test request through each published route monthly and confirm it lands in the case queue with an acknowledgement inside 24 hours.
Record each route test with its timestamp so the accessibility of the mechanism can be evidenced, not asserted.
checklist.done: each published DPO route is live, matches the details notified to the supervisory authorities, and has a dated monthly route test on file.

checklist.step: Log every inbound request and start the clock at receipt
actions: Create a case within one business day of arrival capturing: receipt date, channel, requester name, claimed relationship (policyholder, claimant, employee, candidate, third party), rights claimed and the wording used.
Set the Art. 12(3) due date to receipt date plus one calendar month at case creation - never at identity-verification date.
Send the acknowledgement stating the request reference, the rights being handled and the one-month deadline.
Split multi-right requests into linked sub-cases so an access request and an erasure request are each tracked to their own outcome.
checklist.done: each request is a logged case within one business day, with the due date computed from receipt and an acknowledgement sent.

checklist.step: Sweep the non-DSAR channels for hidden requests
actions: Run a weekly keyword search over call transcripts, chat logs and the complaints queue for phrases such as 'copy of my data', 'delete my data', 'stop using my information', 'GDPR' and their local-language equivalents.
Have the supervisor listen to each hit and decide whether a rights request was made, then raise a case back-dated to the original contact date.
Brief the Contact Center Supervisor to route any such contact straight into the DSAR queue rather than resolving it in the call.
Report the weekly hit count and the number of back-dated cases to the Privacy Officer.
checklist.done: every week's channel sweep is completed and any request found is a case dated from the original contact, with the count reported.

checklist.step: Verify identity proportionately under Art. 12(6)
actions: Check first whether the requester is already authenticated - a portal-authenticated policyholder needs no further proof.
Where doubt exists, request the minimum needed: confirmation of two data points already held (policy number and date of birth), or one photo identity document viewed and not retained beyond the case.
Never demand a certified passport copy as a default; record the reason any documentary proof was required.
Where the request comes from a solicitor, broker or family member, obtain a signed authority naming the data subject and the scope, and check it against the file.
checklist.done: identity is verified by the least intrusive means that resolves the doubt, and the reason for any documentary demand is recorded on the case.

checklist.step: Scope the request and build a documented search plan
actions: Ask the requester, where the request is broad, whether they want a specific period, policy, claim or interaction - and record that Art. 12 clarification does not stop the clock unless the request genuinely cannot be actioned without it.
List every system in scope from the RoPA: policy administration, claims, CRM, billing, the data warehouse, call recordings, email and file shares, and any processor holding the data.
Name a search custodian per system with a due date at least 10 days before the response deadline.
Record the search terms and identifiers used per system so the search can be re-performed by someone else.
checklist.done: a written search plan names every in-scope system, its custodian, its search terms and a due date ahead of the response deadline.

checklist.step: Retrieve the data from each system of record
actions: Run the identifier-based extract across the linked party record so aliases, prior addresses and duplicate customer ids are pulled together.
Pull structured records - policy, endorsement, billing, claim, payment - plus derived data such as rating factors and fraud scores, which are personal data too.
Request unstructured material from custodians: claim notes, adjuster diary entries, emails, call recordings and letters, and log what each custodian returned and when.
Where a processor holds data, invoke the Art. 28(3)(e) assistance clause in the DPA and give the processor a deadline that fits inside the one-month window.
checklist.done: every in-scope system and processor has returned a dated extract or a documented nil return.

checklist.step: Apply exemptions and redact with a stated reason per item
actions: Assess third-party data under Art. 15(4) - redact other individuals' data unless they consent or disclosure is reasonable in all the circumstances, and record which test was applied.

Assess legal professional privilege, litigation material and anti-fraud investigation material under the applicable member-state or UK derogation and cite the provision relied on for each withheld item.
Redact per item with a reason code on the redaction log; a blanket 'third party' across a bundle is not an assessment.
Where the whole request is refused as manifestly unfounded or excessive under Art. 12(5), write out the reasoning and record that the burden of proving it sits with the controller.
checklist.done: every withheld or redacted item carries a cited exemption and a reason code on the redaction log, signed by counsel.

checklist.step: Take the extension decision before day 20 where it is needed
actions: At day 20, review each open case against the Art. 12(3) extension test: complexity of the request or the number of requests from that subject.

Where the test is met, write to the data subject inside the first month stating the extension, the new date (up to two further months) and the specific reasons - volume of claim files, multiple policies, processor retrieval.
Where the test is not met, escalate the resourcing problem to the DPO rather than extending - a resourcing shortfall is not a lawful extension ground.
Record the extension letter and the new due date on the case so the SLA clock re-baselines.
checklist.done: each extended case has a reasoned extension letter sent inside the first month and a re-baselined due date on the case.

checklist.step: Build the response pack and second-review it
actions: Assemble the pack: covering letter answering each right claimed, the Art. 15(1)(a)-(h) supplementary information (purposes, categories, recipients, retention, rights, source, automated decision-making logic), the data itself and an index of documents provided and withheld.
Have a second Privacy Ops reviewer who did no redaction re-open every redaction and confirm the reason code fits the material.
Check every page for stray third-party data left visible - names in email threads and claimant contact details are the usual misses.
Confirm the pack states the right to complain to the Irish DPC or the ICO and the right to a judicial remedy.
checklist.done: the pack is complete, second-reviewed page by page, and states the complaint and judicial-remedy routes.

checklist.step: Deliver the response securely and prove delivery
actions: Issue the pack by secure portal message or password-protected transfer, with the password sent by a separate channel; use tracked post only where no digital route exists.

Where the request came electronically, provide the data in a commonly used electronic form as Art. 12(3) requires, and for portability requests use a structured, machine-readable format such as CSV or JSON per Art. 20(1).
Record the delivery timestamp and the delivery proof reference on the case and stop the SLA clock on that timestamp.
Treat a misdirected pack as a personal data breach and hand it straight to the incident process.
checklist.done: the response is delivered by a secure route with a recorded delivery proof and a stopped SLA clock.

checklist.step: Execute erasure, rectification and restriction in the source systems
actions: For upheld erasure requests, run the deletion or de-identification routine in every system holding the record and capture the job id and record counts.

Where erasure is refused because the data is needed for an open claim, the establishment or defence of legal claims, or a statutory retention duty, cite the Art. 17(3) ground and tell the subject which one applies.
For restriction under Art. 18, apply the system flag that blocks further processing while leaving storage intact, and confirm downstream extracts respect the flag.
For rectification and erasure, notify every recipient the data was disclosed to under Art. 19 and record the notification list, or record why it is impossible or disproportionate.
checklist.done: the source systems reflect the outcome, the Art. 19 recipient notifications are recorded, and every refusal cites an Art. 17(3) ground.

checklist.step: Handle objections and Art. 22 automated-decision requests
actions: For direct-marketing objections under Art. 21(2), suppress the subject across every outbound channel immediately - there is no balancing test to run.
For Art. 21(1) objections to legitimate-interest processing, document the compelling legitimate grounds assessment or stop the processing, and give the subject the reasoning.

For Art. 22 requests on automated underwriting or pricing decisions, arrange human intervention by an underwriter with authority to change the decision, and record the reviewer, the date and the outcome.
Give the subject meaningful information about the logic involved and the significance and consequences, per Art. 15(1)(h).
checklist.done: every objection has a recorded outcome and every Art. 22 request has a named human reviewer with authority and a recorded decision.

checklist.step: Report the DSAR portfolio to the DPO monthly
actions: Publish a monthly view of volumes by right and jurisdiction, cases open by age band (0-15, 16-30, 31-60, 60+ days), extensions used and refusals issued.
List by name every case within 5 days of its deadline and every case past it, with owner and blocker.
Trend the refusal rate and the extension rate - a rising extension rate usually signals a retrieval bottleneck, not complexity.
Table the report at the monthly Privacy Committee with the actions agreed against each overdue case.
checklist.done: a monthly portfolio report is published, named overdue cases carry owners and blockers, and the committee minutes record the agreed actions.

checklist.step: Retain the DSAR case file under the retention rule
actions: Move each closed case file - request, identity evidence, search plan, custodian returns, redaction log, response pack and delivery proof - into the repository under REG-020-C02 and the case reference.
Apply the 6-years-from-closure retention label and confirm the identity documents inside the case were disposed of once verification completed.
Confirm the file is retrievable by requester name, case reference, right claimed and receipt date.
Run a quarterly disposal review so cases past retention are destroyed on schedule and the destruction is logged.
checklist.done: every closed case is filed, labelled for 6-year retention, searchable by requester and reference, and identity documents are disposed of.

checklist.step: Log breaches of the SLA and take counsel sign-off
actions: Raise an exception for each response issued after its due date, each request found outside the log and each refusal without a cited exemption.
Assign root cause (channel not monitored, identity verification used to stall the clock, processor retrieval late, redaction rework) and a named owner.
Sign off the corrective wording sent to any affected subject and decide whether the pattern warrants proactive contact with the supervisory authority.
Carry every open exception into the next quarter's test as a mandatory retest row.
checklist.done: every SLA breach and unsupported refusal has an issue with root cause, owner, counsel sign-off and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Build the population of rights requests received in the quarter
actions: Extract every case with a receipt date inside the quarter, with fields: channel, receipt date, right claimed, jurisdiction, due date, response date, extension flag and outcome.
Add cases opened in prior quarters that were still open at quarter end so ageing is not truncated.
Confirm each right claimed is counted separately where a request covered several rights.
Sign the extract as complete and record the query and row count in the workpaper.
testing.done: a signed population extract covers every request received or open in the quarter, split by right and jurisdiction.

testing.step: Reconcile the log to the inbound channels to find unlogged requests
actions: Independently search the DPO mailbox, the webform submission table, contact-centre transcripts and the complaints register for the same rights keywords the operational sweep uses, plus local-language variants.
Match each hit to a case in the log by requester and date; list every hit with no case.
For each unlogged request, compute how many days it sat unactioned and whether a response was ever sent.
Treat any unlogged request as an automatic exception regardless of whether the subject was eventually answered.
testing.done: every channel hit is matched to a logged case or listed as an unlogged-request exception with its unactioned day count.

testing.step: Draw and document the sample
actions: Take 100% of refusals, 100% of extended cases and 100% of cases closed after their due date.
Take 30 further cases at random with a recorded seed, stratified across access, erasure, rectification, restriction, portability and objection, and across EU and UK.
Record population size, seed, strata and draw date so the sample is reproducible.
Where a right has fewer than 5 cases in the quarter, test that right 100%.
testing.done: a reproducible sample covers all refusals, extensions and late cases plus a stratified random draw across rights and jurisdictions.

testing.step: Recompute the one-month clock and the extension validity
actions: For each sampled case recompute due date = receipt date plus one calendar month, using the original inbound timestamp from the channel, not the case-creation date.
Compare the recomputed due date to the recorded due date and flag any case where the clock was started from identity verification or from case creation.
For extended cases, confirm the extension letter left inside the first month, states specific reasons and sets a date no more than two further months out.
Compute elapsed days to the delivery proof timestamp and list every case answered late, with the overrun in days.
testing.done: the clock is recomputed for every sampled case, late-started clocks are flagged, and each extension is tested for timing and reasoning.

testing.step: Re-perform the search on a subset of access cases
actions: Take 8 sampled access cases and re-run the identifier search independently across policy, claims, CRM, billing and the warehouse using the subject's linked party id and known aliases.
Compare the record counts returned to the custodian returns held on the case file and investigate any system that returned data now but a nil return then.
Check whether derived data - rating factors, propensity or fraud scores - was included in the response, since these are frequently omitted.
Confirm processors named in the RoPA for that processing were actually tasked and returned data.
testing.done: each re-performed search reconciles to the custodian returns or the omission is documented as an exception with the systems named.

testing.step: Re-review redactions and refusals against the cited exemption
actions: Open the unredacted source alongside the issued pack for 10 sampled cases and read each redaction against its reason code.
Test Art. 15(4) third-party redactions - confirm the reasonableness assessment was made rather than a blanket withholding, and that the subject's own data was not redacted with it.
For each refusal, read the cited derogation and confirm it covers the material and the jurisdiction, and that the burden-of-proof reasoning for any Art. 12(5) refusal is written out.
Flag as a fail any redaction whose reason code does not fit the material, and any refusal with no citation.
testing.done: every sampled redaction and refusal is re-read against its cited exemption and mismatches are recorded as fails.

testing.step: Trace outcomes into the source systems
actions: For sampled erasure cases, query the source systems for the subject identifier and confirm the record is gone or de-identified, and read the deletion job id and record count on the case.
For restriction cases, confirm the restriction flag is set and pull a downstream extract to prove the flag is honoured outside the source system.
For rectification cases, confirm the corrected value is live and that the Art. 19 recipient notification list exists.
For marketing objections, confirm suppression across every outbound list and check no send went to the subject after the objection date.
testing.done: each sampled outcome is proven in the source systems and downstream, or the gap is recorded as an exception.

testing.step: Test the accessibility of the published DPO contact routes
actions: Submit a test request through each published route - website webform, DPO mailbox, postal address, portal secure message and the contact-centre script - and time the acknowledgement.
Confirm the DPO contact shown in the current privacy notices matches the details notified to the Irish DPC and the ICO.
Check the route is reachable without logging in and without an account, since non-customers such as third-party claimants must be able to use it.
Capture each submission and acknowledgement into the workpaper with timestamps.
testing.done: every published route accepted a test request, acknowledged it, and matches the contact details notified to the supervisory authorities.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one issue per exception naming the case reference, the failure (late response, mis-started clock, invalid extension, unsupported refusal, incomplete search, outcome not executed) and the subjects affected.
Assign root cause - channel not monitored, clock started at verification, processor retrieval late, redaction rework, deletion routine not covering a system - and a named owner.
Set a remediation date and, where the failure pattern is systemic, ask the Data Protection Officer to decide whether the supervisory authority is told proactively.
Carry every open issue into the next quarter's test as a mandatory retest row.
testing.done: every exception has an issue with root cause, owner, affected-subject count, remediation date and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Compute the on-time response rate, the unlogged-request count, the extension rate and the unsupported-refusal count against the stated thresholds.
Write the conclusion - effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective - citing the workpaper reference behind each figure.
Have the Internal Auditor, who handled no sampled case, sign the workpaper as independent reviewer.
Report to the Data Protection Officer and the Privacy Committee at its next sitting and file the workpaper under REG-020-C02 in the compliance evidence repository.
testing.done: a signed workpaper with a stated conclusion, the four computed measures and a dated committee reporting entry is filed in the evidence repository.

Accountable obligation owner.value: Privacy Office owns the Art. 30 register as controller and as processor; each business Data Steward owns the accuracy of their own activity rows and Privacy Counsel owns the Art. 6 and Art. 9(2) determinations

Citation verified against current regula.value: Yes - GDPR Art. 30(1)-(5) for register content, Art. 6(1) and Art. 5(1)(a) for lawful basis and fairness, Art. 9(1)-(2) for health, biometric and genetic data with the member-state condition under Art. 9(4), Art. 10 for conviction data, and Art. 22/Recital 71 for automated underwriting; read on EUR-Lex and cross-checked to the national insurance derogation relied on in each covered market

In-scope processes.value: Every processing activity in the operating model - underwriting and medical evidence, claims handling and medical reports, fraud and SIU screening, pricing and profiling models, marketing, distribution, HR and occupational health - held as controller, joint controller or processor, in the EU and the UK

In-scope systems.value: Art. 30 register maintained in the GRC platform Privacy module, mapped to physical data locations catalogued in the data catalog/quality tool and to the underwriting, claims, fraud and warehouse platforms that hold the data

Compliance procedure documented.value: Records of Processing Procedure - activity intake, Art. 30(1) field set, lawful-basis determination, Art. 9(2)/Art. 10 condition assessment with the national law cited, special-category data-flow mapping, quarterly steward attestation and the pre-processing gate that blocks a new activity without a register entry

Compliance procedure approved.value: Approved by the Data Protection Officer and the Chief Data Officer; the lawful-basis methodology re-approved annually and on any change to a national insurance derogation

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: No periodic filing - the register must be complete and current at all times and produced to a supervisory authority on request under Art. 30(4); a register entry with a determined Art. 9(2) condition must exist before processing begins, and steward attestation runs on a quarterly cycle

Deadline reminders configured.value: Quarterly attestation tasks issued to every activity owner with a 15-working-day return, escalation to the Data Protection Officer at day 20; a change-management hook raises a register-update task whenever a new data source, model or processor is onboarded

Evidence retained per the retention requ.value: Dated register versions, lawful-basis and Art. 9(2) determination memos, legitimate-interest assessments and quarterly attestations retained 7 years from the date the activity is retired, so the basis in force at any past date is reconstructable

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: Any live processing found without a register entry, any special-category activity without a determined Art. 9(2) condition, and any register field left stale past attestation is logged as a privacy exception with root cause, owner and remediation date

Remediation sign-off captured.value: The DPO signs the register baseline each quarter and every remediation closing an unlawful-basis or unregistered-activity finding, including whether processing is suspended pending the fix

Test population (in-scope transactions,.value: All processing activities in the Art. 30 register plus all data assets in the catalogue that contain personal data, with the special-category subset (health, biometric, genetic, conviction) tested in full

Pass/fail thresholds.value: Zero live processing without a register entry; 100% of special-category activities carry a named Art. 9(2) condition with the member-state law cited; every Art. 30(1)(a)-(g) field populated on every entry; more than 5% of entries stale past their attestation date makes the control ineffective

Compliance test frequency matched to the.value: The obligation is continuous, so completeness monitoring runs quarterly against the catalogue and the change pipeline, with a full lawful-basis re-performance annually and an immediate test whenever a new data source or model goes live

Independent reviewer (segregated from th.value: Auditor must not own, attest or maintain any sampled register entry

Evidence location for test results.value: Quarterly RoPA completeness and lawful-basis workpaper (register export, catalogue reconciliation, sample, determination re-performance notes, exception log) in the compliance evidence repository under REG-020-C03

Regulator-ready documentation.value: Art. 30 register export in writing and electronic form, with the Art. 9(2) determination memos and national-law citations attached, producible to the Irish DPC or the ICO within 5 business days as Art. 30(4) contemplates

Regulator response path.value: The Data Protection Officer produces the register to the supervisory authority; Privacy Counsel clears any determination memo before release and handles challenges to the national insurance derogation relied on

checklist.step: Baseline the activity inventory from the business, not from the old register
actions: Run a structured interview per function - Underwriting Director / Manager, Claims Director / Manager, SIU Manager, Head of Distribution, Chief HR Officer's delegate - listing what personal data they use and for what decision.
Compare the interview output line by line to the current register and list activities present in the business but absent from the register.
Add newly identified activities as draft entries with an owner and a 15-working-day completion date.
Retire entries for activities the business has stopped, recording the stop date rather than deleting the row.
checklist.done: the register reflects the business as described by its own function heads, with additions and retirements dated.

checklist.step: Populate every Art. 30(1) field on each entry
actions: Complete for each activity: controller name and contact and the DPO contact; purposes of processing; categories of data subjects and of personal data; categories of recipients including processors and any third-country recipient; transfers outside the EEA with the country and the Art. 46 safeguard; envisaged retention period per category; and a general description of the technical and organisational security measures under Art. 32(1).
Replace any 'various' or 'to be confirmed' entry with the concrete value; those two strings are the register's most common defect.
Add the Art. 30(2) processor-side fields for activities where the company acts as processor for another controller, naming that controller.
Reject the entry back to the owner where the retention period is not expressed as a number of years from a defined trigger.
checklist.done: no register entry has an empty or placeholder Art. 30(1) or Art. 30(2) field, and every retention period is a number from a defined trigger.

checklist.step: Determine and document the Art. 6 lawful basis per purpose
actions: Set the basis per purpose, not per activity: contract performance for quoting, underwriting and claims payment; legal obligation for sanctions screening, tax and regulatory reporting; legitimate interests for fraud detection and portfolio analytics; consent only where nothing else fits.
Write a legitimate-interest assessment for every Art. 6(1)(f) purpose recording the interest, the necessity test and the balancing outcome, and attach it to the entry.
Record that consent, where relied on, meets Art. 7 - freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, withdrawable - and that the withdrawal route exists in the system.
Confirm the stated basis matches what the privacy notice for that collection point tells the data subject, and raise a defect where they differ.
checklist.done: every purpose has a single named Art. 6 basis, an attached LIA where legitimate interests is used, and agreement with the published notice.

checklist.step: Identify every special-category and conviction data flow
actions: Run the classification scan across the underwriting, claims, medical-evidence and fraud data stores for health, biometric, genetic and conviction attributes, including free-text fields such as adjuster notes and medical summaries.
Map each detected attribute to the register entry that should cover it and list detections with no matching entry.
Tag the physical tables, columns and document stores so the classification is visible to engineering, not only to Privacy.
Re-run the scan monthly and after every schema change so newly added medical or conviction fields surface within the month.
checklist.done: every physical location holding special-category or conviction data is classified, tagged and tied to a register entry.

checklist.step: Determine the Art. 9(2) condition before processing starts
actions: For each special-category activity, select and write out the condition: explicit consent under Art. 9(2)(a), establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims under Art. 9(2)(f), or substantial public interest under Art. 9(2)(g).

Where Art. 9(2)(g) is used, cite the member-state law that provides it and confirm it contains the suitable and specific safeguards Art. 9(2)(g) requires - a bare assertion of public interest is not a condition.
For Art. 10 conviction data used in motor and fraud screening, cite the domestic law authorising the processing under official authority, per market.
Record the determination date, the author and the review date, and block the activity from going live until the memo is on the entry.
checklist.done: every special-category and conviction activity carries a dated, authored condition memo citing the specific national law relied on.

checklist.step: Gate new processing so nothing goes live without an entry
actions: Add a mandatory privacy gate to the change workflow: no epic touching personal data can move to 'Ready for release' without a linked register entry id.
Wire the same gate into the vendor onboarding path so a new processor cannot be contracted without the entry naming it as a recipient.
Wire it into the model release path so a new pricing, propensity or fraud model cannot deploy without the entry recording the profiling purpose.
Review the weekly list of gate overrides with the Data Protection Officer and close each one within the month.
checklist.done: the release, vendor and model paths all block on a linked register entry, and every override is reviewed and closed within a month.

checklist.step: Record automated decision-making and profiling on the entry
actions: List every model that scores an individual - automated underwriting acceptance, risk pricing, propensity, claims triage, fraud score - and link each to its register entry.
For each, record whether the output produces a decision with legal or similarly significant effect under Art. 22(1), and what human involvement actually exists.
Write the meaningful-information-about-the-logic summary that Art. 15(1)(h) demands, in language a data subject can read, and store it with the model card.
Record the safeguards required by Art. 22(3) and Recital 71 - right to human intervention, to express a view, to contest - and where in the process each is delivered.
checklist.done: every scoring model is linked to a register entry with its Art. 22 status, human-involvement description, logic summary and safeguards recorded.

checklist.step: Map recipients, processors and joint controllers per entry
actions: List for each activity the actual recipients: reinsurers, loss adjusters, medical reporting agencies, anti-fraud databases, claims service providers, brokers, regulators.
Mark each as processor, independent controller or joint controller, and for joint controllers record the Art. 26 arrangement reference.
Cross-check every processor named here against the executed DPA register so a recipient without a contract surfaces immediately.
Record the transfer country and safeguard for any recipient outside the EEA and hand the gap list to the Third-Party Risk Manager.
checklist.done: every recipient on every entry is typed, contract-linked, and carries a transfer country and safeguard where it sits outside the EEA.

checklist.step: Set the retention rule per data category and prove it is enforced
actions: Express each retention period as a number of years from a defined trigger - policy expiry, claim closure, last customer contact - and cite the statutory or limitation-period source behind it.
Confirm a purge or archive job exists for each retention rule, naming the system and the schedule, per Art. 5(1)(e) storage limitation.
Where medical evidence is held longer than the policy record, state the separate rule and the reason on the entry.
List rules with no enforcement job and hand them to the Data Platform Engineer with a due date.
checklist.done: every retention rule has a defined trigger, a cited source and either a named enforcement job or a dated remediation owner.

checklist.step: Test that collection is minimised to the declared purpose
actions: For each intake form and pipeline, list the fields actually captured and compare them to the data categories the register entry declares necessary for the purpose.
Flag every field captured but not declared - the classic offenders are full date of birth where age band suffices, full bank details on quote, and free-text medical detail on FNOL.
Raise a change request to remove or stop persisting each excess field, with the system owner named and a date.
Re-test the form or pipeline after release and record the field list before and after.
checklist.done: no intake form or pipeline captures a field outside its register entry's declared categories, or the excess field has a dated removal ticket.

checklist.step: Run the quarterly steward attestation
actions: Receive the attestation task listing your entries and confirm, field by field, that purposes, data categories, recipients, transfers, retention and security description still describe reality.
Where anything changed, edit the entry and state what changed and when, rather than attesting to a stale row.
Confirm no new data source, processor or model was added to your activity without a register update, and list any that were.
Return the attestation inside 15 working days; the platform escalates non-returns to the Data Protection Officer at day 20.
checklist.done: every entry carries a dated attestation from its steward for the quarter, or an escalation record explaining why not.

checklist.step: Reconcile the register to the data catalogue
actions: Export the catalogue's personal-data-classified assets and the register's system list and match them both ways.
List catalogued assets holding personal data with no register entry - these are unregistered processing until proven otherwise.
List register entries naming systems that do not exist in the catalogue - usually a retired system or a wrong system name.
Assign each unmatched item to an owner with a 30-day close date and re-run the reconciliation the following month.
checklist.done: the two-way match is complete and every unmatched asset or entry has an owner and a 30-day close date.

checklist.step: Version and baseline the register each quarter
actions: Export the register in writing and in electronic form as Art. 30(3) requires, named RoPA-<jurisdiction>-<yyyy-Qn>, and lock it.
Attach the quarter's attestation returns, condition memos and LIAs to the baseline so the basis in force at that date is reconstructable.
Record the change log against the previous baseline - entries added, retired and materially amended.
Apply the 7-years-from-activity-retirement retention label to the baseline.
checklist.done: a locked, dated quarterly baseline exists with its supporting memos, change log and retention label.

checklist.step: Report register health to the Privacy Committee
actions: Publish entry count by function, attestation completion rate, count of entries with any empty Art. 30 field, and count of special-category entries without a condition memo.
Name the unregistered activities found by the catalogue reconciliation and the owner of each.
Show the trend in gate overrides, since a rising override count predicts the next unregistered activity.
Table the pack at the quarterly Privacy Committee and minute the decisions, including any processing suspended pending a lawful basis.
checklist.done: the committee has a dated pack showing completeness, attestation and condition-memo coverage, with named owners for every gap.

checklist.step: Log unregistered processing and unlawful-basis findings
actions: Raise an exception for each live activity with no entry, each special-category activity with no Art. 9(2) condition and each entry stale past attestation.
Decide and record for each whether processing continues under a written risk acceptance, is corrected, or is suspended until a basis is established.
Assign root cause (release bypassed the gate, model deployed without review, new data source onboarded silently, steward turnover) and a named owner.
Sign the closure only once the register entry is complete and the classification scan shows the data where the entry says it is.
checklist.done: every unregistered or unsupported activity has a logged exception, a continue-correct-suspend decision, a root cause and a DPO-signed closure.

testing.step: Build the population of processing activities and personal-data assets
actions: Export the full Art. 30 register with all fields, entry owner, last attestation date and status, for EU and UK.
Export the data catalogue's list of assets classified as containing personal data, with system, schema and classification date.
Export the quarter's change records for new systems, new processors and new models from the release and vendor pipelines.
Sign all three extracts as complete and record run dates and row counts.
testing.done: three dated, signed extracts - register, catalogue and change pipeline - are in the workpaper with row counts.

testing.step: Reconcile the register to the catalogue and the change pipeline
actions: Match catalogued personal-data assets to register entries by system and schema and list assets with no entry.
Match every new processor, system and model from the change pipeline to a register entry created or amended on or before its go-live date.
List each unregistered item with its go-live date and the number of days it has been processing without a record.
Treat any item live for more than 30 days without an entry as a reportable finding, not a housekeeping item.
testing.done: both reconciliations are complete and every unregistered asset, processor or model is listed with its days-live figure.

testing.step: Draw and document the sample
actions: Take 100% of entries flagged as involving health, biometric, genetic or Art. 10 conviction data.
Take 100% of entries involving Art. 22 automated decisions or third-country transfers.
Take 25 further entries at random with a recorded seed, stratified across underwriting, claims, fraud, distribution, marketing and HR.
Record population size, seed, strata and draw date so the sample is reproducible.
testing.done: the sample covers all special-category, Art. 22 and transfer entries plus a reproducible stratified random draw.

testing.step: Test Art. 30 field completeness on the sample
actions: Build a grid of the Art. 30(1)(a)-(g) fields, and Art. 30(2) where the company is processor, against each sampled entry.
Mark a field incomplete where it is blank, says 'various', 'as needed' or 'to be confirmed', or names a category rather than the actual recipients.
Check the retention period is a number from a defined trigger with a cited source rather than a narrative.
Compute the field-completeness rate and list every incomplete field by entry and owner.
testing.done: every sampled entry has a completed field grid and the completeness rate is computed with defects listed by owner.

testing.step: Re-perform the Art. 9(2) and Art. 10 condition determination
actions: For each special-category entry, read the condition memo and then read the cited member-state law text yourself before comparing conclusions.
Confirm an Art. 9(2)(g) claim is backed by a law that actually names the processing and provides suitable and specific safeguards, not by a general public-interest statement.
Confirm any Art. 9(2)(a) explicit consent claim is matched by a consent record captured by a separate affirmative action, and that withdrawal is operable.
For Art. 10 entries, confirm the domestic authority cited covers the market where the screening actually happens - a UK authority does not cover an Irish book.
testing.done: each condition is independently re-determined against the cited law and every mismatch or unsupported claim is recorded as a fail.

testing.step: Trace three sampled entries into the physical data
actions: For three sampled entries, query the named systems and profile the columns actually populated for a handful of subject records.
Compare the observed data categories to the categories the entry declares and list anything present but undeclared - especially free-text medical detail and conviction flags.
Confirm the data physically sits in the countries the entry states, by reading the storage region of the tables and buckets involved.
Record the queries used so the trace can be repeated.
testing.done: each traced entry is proven against the physical data, with undeclared categories and location mismatches listed.

testing.step: Test the data-minimisation pass condition on live intake
actions: Take 6 live intake forms and pipelines across quote, application, FNOL and marketing capture and list every field captured.
Compare field by field to the declared necessary categories on the corresponding register entry.
Record each captured-but-undeclared field with the screen or endpoint name and whether the value is persisted.
Fail the item where any pipeline or form captures a field beyond the declared purpose, in line with the stated pass condition.
testing.done: every tested form and pipeline has a field-by-field comparison and any excess field is recorded against its screen or endpoint.

testing.step: Test attestation currency and gate effectiveness
actions: Compute the proportion of entries with an attestation inside the last quarter and list stale entries with the days since last attestation.
Pull the release-gate override log and test 10 overrides to see whether a register entry followed within the month.
Check steward turnover - entries whose named owner has left are usually the stale ones - and list orphaned entries.
Compare the stale rate to the 5% ineffectiveness threshold.
testing.done: the stale rate is computed against the 5% threshold, overrides are tested for follow-up and orphaned entries are listed.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one issue per exception naming the entry or asset, the failure (unregistered activity, missing condition memo, incomplete field, excess field captured, stale attestation) and the data categories involved.
Assign root cause - gate bypassed, model deployed without review, source onboarded silently, steward departed, memo never written - and a named owner.
Set a remediation date and, where special-category data is processed with no condition, ask the Data Protection Officer to decide on suspension.
Carry every open issue into the next quarter's test as a mandatory retest row.
testing.done: every exception has an issue with root cause, owner, remediation date, a suspension decision where required, and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Compute the unregistered-activity count, the Art. 30 field-completeness rate, the special-category condition-coverage rate and the attestation stale rate against the stated thresholds.
Write the conclusion - effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective - citing the workpaper reference behind each figure.
Have the Internal Auditor, who owns and attests no sampled entry, sign the workpaper as independent reviewer.
Report to the Data Protection Officer and the Privacy Committee at its next sitting and file the workpaper under REG-020-C03 in the compliance evidence repository.
testing.done: a signed workpaper with a stated conclusion, the four computed rates and a dated committee reporting entry is filed in the evidence repository.

Accountable obligation owner.value: Procurement / Legal owns execution of every DPA and its audit-rights clause; the Third-Party Risk Manager owns exercising those rights during the contract term and Privacy Counsel owns any deviation from the approved clause set

Citation verified against current regula.value: Yes - GDPR Art. 28(1)-(4) and Art. 28(3)(a)-(h) for the mandatory processor terms including the Art. 28(3)(h) audit and inspection right, Art. 29 on processing only on instruction, Art. 32 security, Art. 5(1)(e) deletion at end of service, and Chapter V Art. 44-49 for transfers; SCC wording checked against Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 modules and, for UK flows, the ICO International Data Transfer Addendum

In-scope processes.value: Vendor onboarding, contract execution, renewal and offboarding for every processor and sub-processor touching personal data - claims service providers, loss adjusters, medical reporting agencies, SaaS platforms, cloud hosting, print and mail houses, offshore BPO, data enrichment and anti-fraud databases - across the EU and the UK

In-scope systems.value: DPAs authored, negotiated and executed in the CLM with clause-level metadata; vendor onboarding and spend in Coupa / SAP Ariba; signature via DocuSign; audit-rights exercises tracked in the GRC platform third-party module

Compliance procedure documented.value: Processor Contracting Procedure - privacy triage at intake, mandatory Art. 28(3) clause set, approved audit-rights language, sub-processor authorisation and notice mechanism, transfer-mechanism selection and transfer impact assessment, and the once-per-term audit-rights exercise

Compliance procedure approved.value: Approved by the General Counsel and the Data Protection Officer; the clause set re-approved annually and immediately on any new EDPB transfer guidance or replacement of the SCC decision

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: DPA executed before any personal data is disclosed - no data flows on a purchase order alone; sub-processor change notice period per contract (30 days is the standard objection window); at least one audit-rights exercise or assessment per contract term; deletion or return certificate within 30 days of termination

Deadline reminders configured.value: CLM alerts at 180, 90 and 30 days before each DPA expiry; a term-half-way task to schedule the audit-rights exercise; a 30-day countdown task on every termination for the deletion certificate; watchlist alert on any sub-processor notice received

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: Any live data flow without an executed DPA, any DPA missing an Art. 28(3) term, any unapproved sub-processor and any contract term ending without an audit-rights exercise is logged with root cause, vendor owner and remediation date

Remediation sign-off captured.value: Counsel signs off every deviation from the approved Art. 28(3) clause set, every transfer mechanism selection and every remediation closing a missing-DPA or unexercised-audit-right finding
