checklist.step: Triage every new vendor for personal-data processing at intake
actions: Make the privacy triage questions mandatory on the supplier request form: will the vendor access, receive, store or be able to see personal data; whose data; special-category or conviction data; from which countries; hosted where.
Block the requisition from progressing to sourcing where any answer is yes and no privacy assessment is attached.
Route yes-answers to the Third-Party Risk Manager and the Privacy Officer the same day with the data categories and volumes described.
Record the triage answers on the vendor master so the flag persists to renewal.
checklist.done: no requisition involving personal data progresses without a triage record and a routed privacy assessment.

checklist.step: Fix the controller/processor characterisation before drafting
actions: Decide, from who determines purposes and means, whether the vendor is a processor, an independent controller (a reinsurer or a regulator recipient often is) or a joint controller.
Write the reasoning on the matter file - the wrong characterisation produces the wrong contract and is the most common root defect.
For joint controllers, require an Art. 26 arrangement setting out respective responsibilities and the essence made available to data subjects.
For independent controllers, require a data-sharing agreement with transfer terms rather than an Art. 28 DPA.
checklist.done: each vendor has a written characterisation with reasoning that drives which contract type is issued.

checklist.step: Issue the approved Art. 28(3) clause set
actions: Generate the DPA from the approved template so all eight Art. 28(3) terms are present: process only on documented instructions; confidentiality commitments from personnel; Art. 32 security measures; sub-processor conditions; assistance with data-subject rights; assistance with Art. 32-36 obligations including breach notification; deletion or return at end of service; and make available all information necessary to demonstrate compliance and allow for and contribute to audits and inspections.
Complete the Annex describing subject matter, duration, nature and purpose, types of personal data and categories of data subjects, as Art. 28(3) requires - an empty annex voids the specificity.
Tag each clause in the CLM with its Art. 28(3) sub-paragraph so clause-presence can be reported without reading the document.
Send any vendor redline of the clause set to Privacy Counsel; do not accept edits at negotiator level.
checklist.done: the executed DPA carries all eight tagged Art. 28(3) clauses and a completed processing annex.

checklist.step: Harden the audit-rights clause so it can actually be used
actions: Require the clause to permit audits by the controller or an auditor it mandates, on reasonable notice, at least once per contract year and at any time following a personal data breach or a supervisory-authority direction.
Refuse language that limits the right to a certification report only - a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 report may satisfy a cycle but must not extinguish the right to inspect.
Extend the right down the chain so sub-processors are contractually bound to the same audit obligation, and require the vendor to enforce it on request.
Fix cost allocation and the remediation timetable in the clause so a finding has a contractual close date rather than a conversation.
checklist.done: every DPA contains an enforceable audit right covering sub-processors, not extinguished by certifications, with a remediation timetable.

checklist.step: Set the sub-processor authorisation and notice mechanism
actions: Choose specific or general written authorisation under Art. 28(2) and record which applies; where general, fix the notice period for changes at 30 days with a documented objection right.
Require the vendor to publish and maintain a sub-processor list with location and service, and to flow down the same data-protection obligations under Art. 28(4).
Record the sub-processor list as at signature onto the contract record so later changes are detectable.
Register the vendor's notification address in the CLM watchlist so change notices are not lost in a personal mailbox.
checklist.done: the authorisation type, notice period, objection route and the signature-date sub-processor list are recorded on the contract.

checklist.step: Select and paper the transfer mechanism for non-EEA flows
actions: Identify every country where the vendor or its sub-processors store or access the data, including remote support from offshore sites.

Apply the mechanism in order: an adequacy decision under Art. 45 where one covers the country; otherwise SCCs under Art. 46(2)(c) using the correct module (controller-to-processor is Module Two) from Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914; binding corporate rules where the group has them; Art. 49 derogations only for genuinely occasional transfers, never as a standing basis.
For UK flows, append the ICO International Data Transfer Addendum to the EU SCCs or use the IDTA, and record which was used.
Complete the SCC annexes properly - parties, description of transfer, technical and organisational measures, sub-processor list - since blank annexes are the usual audit finding.
checklist.done: every non-EEA flow has a named mechanism with completed annexes and, for UK flows, the addendum or IDTA on file.

checklist.step: Run the transfer impact assessment before the transfer starts
actions: Document the transfer: data categories, volumes, recipients, format, onward transfers and whether the data is encrypted in transit and at rest with keys held in the EEA.
Assess the destination country's law and practice on public-authority access against the EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 essential guarantees.

Where the assessment shows a gap, record the supplementary measures relied on - encryption with controller-held keys, pseudonymisation, split processing, transparency reporting and a challenge commitment - and confirm they are in the contract.
Set a re-assessment date and re-run the TIA if the destination law changes or the vendor changes its hosting.
checklist.done: each transfer has a dated TIA with a documented conclusion, named supplementary measures in the contract, and a re-assessment date.

checklist.step: Complete security due diligence before signature
actions: Collect and read the vendor's current ISO 27001 certificate with its statement of applicability, or the SOC 2 Type II report, checking the scope covers the service being bought and the report period is current.
Read the exceptions section of the SOC 2 report rather than the opinion page, and log every exception as an open item.
Confirm the Art. 32 measures described in the DPA schedule match what the report evidences - encryption, access control, logging, backup, pen-test cadence, breach notification timescales.
Record a residual-risk rating and require the Chief Info Security Officer's acceptance for any high rating before signature.
checklist.done: a dated due-diligence record exists with scoped evidence read, exceptions logged and a risk rating accepted at the right level.

checklist.step: Execute the DPA before any data moves
actions: Route the DPA and its annexes for signature by an authorised signatory on both sides and capture the completed certificate of completion.
Load the executed pack into the CLM against the vendor record with fields: effective date, term end, characterisation, transfer mechanism, audit clause reference and sub-processor authorisation type.
Confirm with the system owner that no interface, extract or credential is enabled until the executed date is recorded - and pull the access if it already is.
Update the Art. 30 register entry to name the processor as a recipient with its location.
checklist.done: the DPA is executed and indexed before any access is granted, and the register entry names the processor.

checklist.step: Maintain the sub-processor register and act on change notices
actions: Log every sub-processor change notice on receipt with the notice date, the sub-processor, its location and the service.
Assess within the objection window whether the change introduces a new country, a new data category or a weaker security posture, and consult the Privacy Officer where it does.
Object in writing before the window closes where the change is unacceptable, and record the vendor's response and the outcome.
Re-check the vendor's published list quarterly against your register so unnotified additions are caught.
checklist.done: every notice is logged, assessed inside the objection window with an outcome, and the quarterly list check is completed.

checklist.step: Exercise the audit right at least once per contract term
actions: Schedule the exercise at the half-way point of the term so a finding can still be remediated inside the contract.

Choose the depth by risk: an evidenced control questionnaire with artifact sampling for low risk, a remote control review for medium, an on-site or third-party-mandated inspection for vendors handling special-category data at volume.

Test the Art. 28(3) obligations specifically - instruction-only processing, personnel confidentiality, sub-processor flow-down, deletion capability and breach notification timelines - not just generic security.
Issue a written report with findings, agreed actions, owners and dates, and file it against the contract record.
checklist.done: every contract term shows at least one dated, scoped audit-rights exercise with a written report and agreed actions.

checklist.step: Track vendor audit findings and breach notifications to closure
actions: Open an issue per finding with severity, contractual clause breached, owner at the vendor and the internal relationship owner.
Chase evidence of remediation rather than assertions - a re-issued policy is not proof a control operates.
Where the vendor notifies a personal data breach, hand it to the incident process the same day so the Art. 33 clock is assessed against the controller's awareness.
Escalate overdue high findings to the Chief Info Security Officer and consider the contractual step-in or termination right.
checklist.done: every audit finding and vendor breach notification has an issue, evidenced remediation and an escalation path where overdue.

checklist.step: Re-paper at renewal against the current clause set
actions: At the 180-day alert, compare the in-force DPA to the current approved clause set and list every gap.
Refresh the transfer mechanism where the SCC decision, the adequacy position or the vendor's hosting changed since signature.
Refresh the processing annex to describe the service as it is now performed, including any scope creep since signature.
Do not auto-renew a contract whose DPA fails the current clause test; escalate to the General Counsel instead.
checklist.done: each renewal either lands on the current clause set and a current transfer mechanism, or is escalated rather than auto-renewed.

checklist.step: Close out deletion or return at termination
actions: On termination, issue the Art. 28(3)(g) instruction stating whether data is to be returned or deleted, in what format and by when.
Require a signed deletion certificate within 30 days naming the systems, environments and backups covered and the date deletion completed.
Confirm the vendor's retention of any copy is limited to what Union or member-state law requires, and get the legal basis for any retained copy in writing.
Disable interfaces, credentials and API keys and confirm the access removal with the Access Management Analyst.
checklist.done: every terminated contract has a signed deletion or return certificate inside 30 days and confirmed access removal.

checklist.step: Log contracting exceptions and take counsel sign-off
actions: Raise an exception for every live data flow without an executed DPA, every missing Art. 28(3) term, every unnotified sub-processor and every term ending with no audit-rights exercise.
Assign root cause (triage skipped at intake, redline accepted at negotiator level, notice sent to a personal mailbox, audit not scheduled) and a named owner.
Decide whether the flow is suspended pending papering, and record the decision and who took it.
Sign the closure only when the executed document or the audit report is attached to the contract record.
checklist.done: every contracting exception has a logged issue, a suspend-or-continue decision, a root cause and a counsel-signed closure with the document attached.

testing.step: Build the population of processors and personal-data flows
actions: Extract all active suppliers with spend in the period and join the privacy triage flag from the vendor master.
Add every processor named as a recipient in the Art. 30 register, since the register and the spend file rarely agree.
Add vendors identified from network egress and integration inventories so unpaid or free-tier processors are not missed.
Sign the merged population as complete and record source systems, run date and row count.
testing.done: a merged, signed processor population exists built from spend, register and integration sources.

testing.step: Reconcile the population to executed DPAs in the CLM
actions: Export all DPAs with vendor, effective date, term end, characterisation, transfer mechanism and audit clause reference.
Match each population vendor to an executed DPA effective on or before the date data first flowed.
List vendors with no DPA, with a DPA effective after data started flowing, and with an expired DPA still receiving data.
Treat each as an automatic exception with the number of days of unpapered processing computed.
testing.done: every processor is matched to a pre-dated executed DPA or listed with its days of unpapered processing.

testing.step: Draw and document the sample
actions: Take 100% of vendors processing special-category or conviction data and 100% of vendors with non-EEA storage or access.
Take 20 further vendors at random with a recorded seed across the remaining population, plus all contracts terminated in the period.
Record population size, seed, strata and draw date so the sample is reproducible.
Note vendors excluded and why - an exclusion list is part of the evidence, not an omission.
testing.done: a reproducible sample covers all high-risk and transfer vendors, terminations and a random tail, with exclusions documented.

testing.step: Test clause presence against Art. 28(3) on the sample
actions: Build a grid with one column per Art. 28(3)(a)-(h) obligation and one row per sampled DPA.
Read the executed document rather than the CLM tag - tags drift from text - and mark each obligation present only where the wording actually creates it.
Test the Art. 28(3)(h) audit right specifically: does it permit inspection, does it extend to sub-processors, is it extinguished by a certification, and does it bind a remediation timetable.
Confirm the processing annex names subject matter, duration, nature, purpose, data types and data-subject categories, and mark it a defect where blank.
testing.done: each sampled DPA has a completed clause grid read from the executed text, with audit-right adequacy separately concluded.

testing.step: Re-perform the transfer-mechanism and TIA review
actions: For each sampled non-EEA vendor, confirm the recorded mechanism matches the actual data locations, including sub-processor and support locations.
Check the SCC module is the right one for the relationship and that the annexes are populated, not left as template placeholders.
For UK flows, confirm the addendum or IDTA is attached and executed.
Read the TIA and confirm it addresses public-authority access in the destination country and that any supplementary measures claimed are actually in the contract or technically in place.
testing.done: each transfer has a mechanism matching real data locations, populated annexes and a TIA whose supplementary measures are verifiable.

testing.step: Test that the audit right was exercised in the term
actions: For each sampled contract, look for at least one exercise or assessment inside the current term and read the report.

Check the exercise tested Art. 28(3) obligations - instruction-only processing, personnel confidentiality, sub-processor flow-down, deletion capability, breach timelines - and not only generic infrastructure security.
Where a certification report was accepted in place of an inspection, confirm its scope covers the bought service and its period covers the term, and read the exceptions section.
List every term with no exercise as a fail against the stated pass condition.
testing.done: each sampled term shows a scoped, dated exercise with Art. 28(3) coverage, or is recorded as a fail.

testing.step: Test sub-processor control end to end
actions: Pull the vendor's currently published sub-processor list and compare it to the register held on the contract record.
List additions never notified and additions notified after the change took effect, with dates.
For 5 additions, confirm an assessment was made inside the objection window and that a new country triggered a transfer-mechanism update.
Confirm the DPA obliges flow-down under Art. 28(4) and that the vendor can evidence it for at least one named sub-processor.
testing.done: the published and held sub-processor lists are reconciled, unnotified or late additions are listed, and flow-down evidence is obtained for a named sub-processor.

testing.step: Test deletion and return at termination
actions: For every contract terminated in the period, look for the signed deletion or return certificate and compute days from termination to certificate against the 30-day rule.
Confirm the certificate names systems, environments and backups rather than making a general assertion.
Confirm interfaces, service accounts and API keys were disabled, by reading the access-removal record in the IAM platform.
Where a copy was retained, read the stated legal requirement and confirm it exists.
testing.done: every termination has a certificate inside 30 days naming systems and backups, with access removal proven and any retained copy justified.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one issue per exception naming the vendor, the failure (no DPA, missing Art. 28(3) term, weak audit right, wrong or missing transfer mechanism, unexercised audit right, unnotified sub-processor, no deletion certificate) and the data categories exposed.
Assign root cause - triage skipped, redline accepted below counsel, notice lost, audit unscheduled, offboarding not run - and a named owner.
Set a remediation date and, where personal data is flowing unpapered, ask the General Counsel to decide on suspension of the flow.
Carry every open issue into the next quarter's test as a mandatory retest row.
testing.done: every exception has an issue with root cause, owner, remediation date, a suspension decision where data flows unpapered, and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Compute the unpapered-flow count, the Art. 28(3) clause-completeness rate, the audit-rights exercise rate per term and the on-time deletion-certificate rate against the stated thresholds.
Write the conclusion - effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective - citing the workpaper reference behind each figure.
Have the Internal Auditor, who negotiated and assessed none of the sampled vendors, sign the workpaper as independent reviewer.
Report to the Data Protection Officer, the General Counsel and the Third-Party Risk Committee at its next sitting and file the workpaper under REG-020-C04 in the compliance evidence repository.
testing.done: a signed workpaper with a stated conclusion, the four computed rates and a dated committee reporting entry is filed in the evidence repository.

checklist.step: Force a DPIA screening at initiative intake
actions: Add a mandatory privacy screening sub-task to every epic created in the change backlog, and block transition out of 'Discovery' until it is answered.

Ask the screening questions in operational terms: does it score or rank individuals, use health or medical evidence, use a new external data source, monitor location or behaviour, process at large scale, or combine datasets held for different purposes.
Route every yes-answer to the Privacy Office queue the same day with the initiative sponsor named.
Reconcile the backlog to the screening list weekly so an epic created outside the standard path is caught within a week.
checklist.done: every personal-data initiative in the backlog has a dated screening record and no epic leaves Discovery without one.

checklist.step: Apply the Art. 35(3) threshold test and the national lists
actions: Test the initiative against Art. 35(3)(a) systematic and extensive automated evaluation producing legal or similarly significant effects, (b) large-scale special-category or Art. 10 data, and (c) systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area.

Then test it against the WP248 nine criteria - evaluation or scoring, automated decision-making, systematic monitoring, sensitive data, large scale, matching or combining datasets, vulnerable data subjects, innovative use of technology, and processing that prevents access to a service or contract.
Then read the Art. 35(4) mandatory list published by the Irish DPC and, for UK processing, the ICO list, and record whether the initiative appears on either.
Record the conclusion with the criteria met; where the conclusion is 'no DPIA required', write the reasoning - two or more WP248 criteria normally means a DPIA is required.
checklist.done: the screening records which Art. 35(3), WP248 and national-list criteria are met and a reasoned required/not-required conclusion.

checklist.step: Describe the processing operations and their necessity
actions: Write the Art. 35(7)(a) systematic description: nature, scope, context and purposes, the data flows end to end, the data categories and subject categories, volumes, retention and recipients including processors and any third-country transfer.
Attach the actual data-flow diagram from the solution architect rather than a prose summary, and name each system by its real name.
Record the legitimate interest pursued where Art. 6(1)(f) is the basis, and link to the register entry that will carry the activity.
Have the Solutions Architect confirm the description matches the design as it will be built, and date that confirmation.
checklist.done: the DPIA carries an architect-confirmed systematic description with a real data-flow diagram, named systems, volumes and recipients.

checklist.step: Assess necessity and proportionality against the purpose
actions: Test each data field against the purpose under Art. 35(7)(b) and strike the ones the purpose does not need - the assessment must record what was removed, not only what was kept.

Test whether a less intrusive alternative achieves the purpose: aggregated instead of individual data, pseudonymised instead of identified, age band instead of date of birth, sampled instead of full population.
Record the lawful basis and, for special-category data, the Art. 9(2) condition with its member-state law, before any processing is designed around it.
Record how transparency, rights delivery and retention will actually operate in the new processing rather than asserting they will.
checklist.done: the necessity and proportionality section names fields removed, alternatives tested, the lawful basis and how rights and retention will operate.

checklist.step: Assess risks to the rights and freedoms of data subjects
actions: Build the risk register from the data-subject's perspective under Art. 35(7)(c) - not the company's: wrongful refusal of cover, mispriced premium from a proxy variable, disclosure of a health condition to a household member, re-identification of pseudonymised claims data, loss of control over telematics location data.
Score each risk for severity and likelihood using the published scale and record the reasoning for the score, not just the number.
Include risks from the processing being unavailable or inaccurate, not only from unauthorised access.
Ask the Model Risk Manager for the model's known bias and drift risks and carry them into the register verbatim.
checklist.done: the risk register lists data-subject-facing risks with scored severity and likelihood and recorded reasoning, including model bias and drift.

checklist.step: Design the mitigations and fix owners and dates
actions: For each risk record the Art. 35(7)(d) measure: pseudonymisation at ingest, field-level encryption, role-based access with claims-adjuster segregation, purpose-bound data marts, automated retention deletion, human review before an adverse decision.
Convert every mitigation into a build task in the delivery backlog with an owner and a target sprint, so the DPIA cannot be satisfied by intention alone.
Score the residual risk after mitigation and record it beside the inherent score.
Where a mitigation cannot be delivered before go-live, say so and let the residual risk stand at its unmitigated level rather than assuming it.
checklist.done: every risk has a named measure, a backlog task with owner and sprint, and an honest residual score.

checklist.step: Take the DPO's Art. 35(2) advice in writing
actions: Review the draft DPIA and issue a written advice note covering whether a DPIA was required, whether it was carried out correctly, and whether the mitigations bring residual risk to an acceptable level.
State plainly where you disagree with the assessor - Art. 39(1)(c) advice is not a countersignature and a recorded disagreement is itself compliance evidence.
Record whether Art. 36 prior consultation is triggered and why.
Date the note and attach it to the assessment; no DPIA closes without it.
checklist.done: a dated DPO advice note is attached stating the required/correct/acceptable conclusions and the prior-consultation decision.

checklist.step: Consult data subjects or their representatives where appropriate
actions: Decide under Art. 35(9) whether to seek the views of data subjects; for telematics, wearable data or claims-triage automation the default should be yes.
Run the consultation through customer research panels, the Consumer Affairs function or a broker or trade-body forum, and keep the questions and the raw responses.
Where consultation is not sought, record the reason - commercial confidentiality or disproportionate effort - as Art. 35(9) contemplates.
Feed the responses into the risk register and record which risks or mitigations changed as a result.
checklist.done: consultation evidence or a recorded reason for not consulting exists, with the resulting changes to the risk register identified.

checklist.step: Take the residual-risk decision from the accountable owner
actions: Review the residual risk scores and the mitigations that will not be in place at go-live.
Accept, reject or condition the processing in writing, naming the conditions and their dates where conditional.
Escalate any residual high risk to the Data Protection Officer for the Art. 36 prior-consultation decision rather than accepting it locally.
Record the acceptance with name, role and date on the DPIA record - an unsigned DPIA is not an approved DPIA.
checklist.done: the DPIA carries a named, dated accept/reject/conditional decision from the accountable owner, with high residual risks escalated.

checklist.step: File Art. 36 prior consultation where residual high risk remains
actions: Prepare the Art. 36(3) submission: respective responsibilities of controller, joint controllers and processors; purposes and means of the processing; the measures and safeguards; the DPO's contact details; the DPIA itself; and any other information the authority requests.

File with the lead supervisory authority - the Irish DPC under the Art. 56 one-stop-shop for EU processing, the ICO for UK-only processing - through its published prior-consultation route, and record the submission reference and date.
Hold the processing: it cannot start before the authority's advice or before the 8-week period, extendable by 6 weeks, has run.
Log every clarification request and response, since Art. 36(2) suspends the period while information is awaited.
checklist.done: the submission is filed with a reference and date, the clock is tracked, and no processing starts before advice or expiry of the period.

checklist.step: Hold the pre-build gate closed until the DPIA is approved
actions: Configure the epic workflow so 'Ready for build' requires a linked DPIA record in Approved status, or a screening conclusion of not-required.
Refuse production personal data in development and test environments until the DPIA's data-handling measures are in place; use synthetic or masked data instead.
Route any override request to the Data Protection Officer and record the business justification and the expiry date of the override.
Review open overrides weekly and close each inside the month.
checklist.done: no epic reaches build with an unapproved DPIA, and every override has a DPO decision, justification and expiry.

checklist.step: Verify the mitigations were actually built before go-live
actions: Take the mitigation list from the approved DPIA and test each one in the pre-production environment: pseudonymisation applied at ingest, encryption keys held where stated, access roles matching the design, retention job scheduled, human-review step present in the decision flow.
Capture evidence per mitigation - a configuration screenshot, a query result, a test case id - rather than a developer's confirmation.
Raise a go-live blocker for any mitigation that scored down a high residual risk and is not in place.
Write the verification result back onto the DPIA record before release approval.
checklist.done: every mitigation is evidenced as built or is a recorded go-live blocker, and the result is written back to the DPIA.

checklist.step: Deliver the Art. 22 safeguards for automated decisions
actions: Where the processing produces a decision with legal or similarly significant effect, confirm the Art. 22(2) exception relied on - contract necessity, member-state law, or explicit consent - and record it.

Build the Art. 22(3) safeguards into the operating process: a named human reviewer with authority and information to change the decision, a route for the subject to express a view, and a route to contest.
Write the meaningful-information-about-the-logic statement for the privacy notice and the DSAR response, per Art. 15(1)(h) and Recital 71.
Record the bias and fairness testing performed and the review cadence, and link it to the model card.
checklist.done: the Art. 22 exception is recorded, the three safeguards are operational, and the logic statement and bias testing are linked to the model card.

checklist.step: Re-review the DPIA on change and at least annually
actions: Set an Art. 35(11) review date on every approved DPIA at 12 months and link it to the model or system change record so a material change pulls the review forward.
Treat these as material changes: new data source, new country of processing, new processor, a model retrained on different data, a purpose extension, or a rise in volume by an order of magnitude.
Re-run the affected sections and re-take the DPO advice and the residual-risk decision - a review is not a date-stamp on the old document.
Record superseded versions so the assessment in force at any past date can be produced.
checklist.done: every approved DPIA has a live review date, material changes pull the review forward, and version history is preserved.

checklist.step: Log DPIA exceptions and take DPO sign-off
actions: Raise an exception for every initiative that built or processed production data without an approved DPIA, every screening not completed, every mitigation not built and every DPIA past its review date.
Decide whether the processing is suspended, run under a written risk acceptance, or corrected before continuing, and record the decision.
Assign root cause - epic created outside the intake path, gate overridden, mitigation dropped in scope-cutting, review date unowned - and a named owner.
Sign the closure only when the approved DPIA and the mitigation evidence are attached.
checklist.done: every DPIA exception has a logged issue, a suspend-accept-correct decision, a root cause and a DPO-signed closure with evidence attached.

testing.step: Build the population of initiatives and model releases
actions: Extract every epic created or transitioned to build in the period, with sponsor, systems touched and the personal-data flag.
Add every model version deployed in the period from the model governance repository, since model retraining rarely appears as an epic.
Add new data-source onboarding records and new processor onboarding records, which also trigger screening.
Sign the merged population as complete and record source systems, run date and row count.
testing.done: a merged, signed population of epics, model releases, data sources and processors exists with counts recorded.

testing.step: Reconcile the population to screening records
actions: Match each population item to a screening record dated on or before its build-start date.
List items with no screening and items screened after build started, with the days of unassessed build computed.
Compare the screening's personal-data answer to the systems the epic actually touched, using the Art. 30 register, and flag any 'no personal data' answer contradicted by the systems involved.
Treat unscreened items as automatic exceptions.
testing.done: every population item is matched to a pre-dated screening or listed with its days of unassessed build.

testing.step: Draw and document the sample
actions: Take 100% of initiatives involving automated decisions with significant effect, special-category data at scale, or a new third country.
Take 100% of screenings concluding 'no DPIA required' where two or more WP248 criteria were ticked - that combination is where the wrong call hides.
Take 15 further initiatives at random with a recorded seed from the remainder.
Record population size, seed, strata and draw date so the sample is reproducible.
testing.done: a reproducible sample covers all high-risk initiatives, all questionable not-required calls and a random tail.

testing.step: Re-perform the threshold determination
actions: Read each sampled initiative's description and reach your own Art. 35(3) and WP248 conclusion before opening the screening record.
Check the Irish DPC and ICO Art. 35(4) lists for the processing type and record whether it appears.
Compare to the recorded conclusion; a difference is an exception, including a right answer supported by the wrong criteria.
Capture the list page or guidance paragraph relied on into the workpaper.
testing.done: each sampled initiative has an independent threshold conclusion with the source captured, and differences are logged.

testing.step: Test DPIA content against the four Art. 35(7) elements
actions: Grid each sampled DPIA against Art. 35(7)(a) systematic description, (b) necessity and proportionality, (c) risks to rights and freedoms and (d) measures to address them.
Mark (c) a defect where the risks are written from the company's perspective - reputational or regulatory risk - rather than the data subject's.
Confirm the DPO advice note exists, is dated before approval, and states a conclusion rather than acknowledging receipt.
Confirm a named accountable owner signed the residual-risk decision and that the signature pre-dates build start.
testing.done: each sampled DPIA has a completed Art. 35(7) grid, a dated substantive DPO advice note and a pre-build signed residual-risk decision.

testing.step: Prove the pre-build gate held
actions: For each sampled initiative, compare the DPIA approval timestamp to the first build commit date in the source code repository and the first production data-processing date.
Check the development and test environments for production personal data before the approval date, using the environment data-classification scan.
Read every gate override raised in the period, its justification, its expiry and whether a DPIA followed inside the month.
Any build or production processing before approval is a reportable breach, not a test exception.
testing.done: the approval-to-build sequence is proven for every sampled initiative and every override is tested for follow-up.

testing.step: Verify the mitigations exist in production
actions: Take 10 mitigations from sampled DPIAs that reduced a high inherent risk and test each in production directly.
For access-control mitigations, pull the entitlement report and confirm the role model matches the DPIA design, including claims-adjuster segregation.
For pseudonymisation, encryption and retention mitigations, query the data store and the scheduler to confirm the transformation and the deletion job actually run.
For human-review mitigations, pull decision records and confirm a named human changed or confirmed decisions with authority to do so.
testing.done: each tested mitigation is evidenced live in production or recorded as an unmitigated risk carried into production.

testing.step: Test prior consultation and the Art. 35(11) review population
actions: List every DPIA closing with residual high risk and confirm an Art. 36 submission exists with its reference, filing date and the authority's response or the expiry of the 8-week (or extended 14-week) period.
Confirm no processing started before that point, by comparing the go-live date to the filing and response dates.
List every approved DPIA past its 12-month review date and every DPIA whose linked model was retrained or whose processing gained a new country or processor without a re-review.
Compute the overdue-review rate and the average days overdue.
testing.done: each residual-high-risk DPIA is traced to a prior-consultation submission and outcome, and the overdue-review population is quantified.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one issue per exception naming the initiative, the failure (no screening, wrong threshold call, missing Art. 35(7) element, build before approval, mitigation not built, no prior consultation, overdue review) and the data subjects exposed.
Assign root cause - epic outside the intake path, gate override never closed, mitigation dropped in scope-cutting, review date unowned - and a named owner.
Set a remediation date and, where processing ran without an approved DPIA, ask the Data Protection Officer to decide on suspension and on supervisory-authority contact.
Carry every open issue into the next quarter's test as a mandatory retest row.
testing.done: every exception has an issue with root cause, owner, remediation date, a suspension decision where required, and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Compute the screening-coverage rate, the build-before-approval count, the Art. 35(7) completeness rate, the mitigation-implementation rate and the overdue-review rate against the stated thresholds.
Write the conclusion - effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective - citing the workpaper reference behind each figure.
Have the Internal Auditor, who authored, advised on and signed no sampled DPIA, sign the workpaper as independent reviewer.
Report to the Data Protection Officer and the Privacy Committee at its next sitting and file the workpaper under REG-020-C05 in the compliance evidence repository.
testing.done: a signed workpaper with a stated conclusion, the five computed rates and a dated committee reporting entry is filed in the evidence repository.

Accountable obligation owner.value: CISO owns detection, containment and the incident record; the Data Protection Officer owns the Art. 33 notifiability decision, the filing to the supervisory authority and the Art. 34 high-risk determination for individual notification

Citation verified against current regula.value: Yes - GDPR Art. 33(1) 72-hour supervisory-authority notification with Art. 33(3)(a)-(d) content, Art. 33(2) processor-to-controller notification, Art. 33(5) internal breach register, and Art. 34(1)-(3) communication to data subjects with its three exemptions; read on EUR-Lex against EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 on personal data breach notification and, for UK incidents, the ICO personal data breach guidance

In-scope processes.value: Detection through SOC monitoring, service desk, claims and contact-centre reporting and processor notification; triage, containment, forensic assessment, risk determination, supervisory-authority notification, individual communication, and post-incident remediation - for policyholder, claimant, employee and broker-client data in the EU and the UK

In-scope systems.value: Detection and case orchestration in the SIEM/SOAR with endpoint telemetry from CrowdStrike Falcon; the incident record and the Art. 33(5) breach register in the GRC platform; supervisory-authority filings made on the Irish DPC breach webform and the ICO breach reporting service; subject notifications issued through the contact centre and mail house

Compliance procedure documented.value: Personal Data Breach Procedure - awareness definition and clock start, 24/7 triage, severity and risk scoring, the 72-hour notification path with phased notification, the Art. 34 high-risk test and its exemptions, processor breach handling, and the Art. 33(5) register entry standard

Compliance procedure approved.value: Approved by the Chief Info Security Officer and the Data Protection Officer, endorsed by the Board Risk Committee; reviewed annually and after every notifiable breach or breach simulation

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: Supervisory authority notified within 72 hours of the controller becoming aware, with reasoned delay explained where later (Art. 33(1)); phased detail supplied as it becomes available (Art. 33(4)); data subjects notified without undue delay where high risk (Art. 34(1)); processors must notify the controller without undue delay (Art. 33(2)), contractually fixed at 24 hours

Deadline reminders configured.value: The 72-hour countdown starts automatically on the awareness timestamp, with automated escalations to the DPO at T+12, T+24 and T+48 hours and a mandatory notify-or-justify decision recorded by T+60; a separate 24-hour clock on any processor-reported breach

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: Every notification filed past 72 hours, every incident where the awareness timestamp was set late, every unregistered breach and every high-risk breach with no subject communication is logged with root cause, owner and remediation date

Remediation sign-off captured.value: The DPO signs every notify/do-not-notify decision with its reasoning, every Art. 34 exemption relied on, and every remediation closing a late-notification finding

Compliance test frequency matched to the.value: The obligation is event-driven, so every notifiable breach gets a post-incident review within 10 working days, with a quarterly test over the whole incident population and a table-top breach simulation each half-year to test the 72-hour path end to end

Regulator-ready documentation.value: Art. 33(5) register export, per-incident chronology with the awareness timestamp evidenced, submitted breach forms with their authority reference numbers, and subject-notification proofs, producible to the Irish DPC or the ICO within 5 business days

checklist.step: Define awareness and start the clock the moment it is met
actions: Write into the procedure that awareness is reached when the controller has a reasonable degree of certainty that a security incident occurred leading to personal data being compromised - not when the investigation finishes.
Make the awareness timestamp a mandatory field on the incident record, defaulted to the moment triage confirmed personal data involvement, with any later value requiring a written reason.
Record separately the detection timestamp, the report timestamp and the awareness timestamp so the gap between them is visible and auditable.
Publish the rule that a short period of initial verification is acceptable but must be counted, not excluded.
checklist.done: every incident record carries detection, report and awareness timestamps, with any delayed awareness justified in writing.

checklist.step: Keep every detection and reporting channel feeding one queue
actions: Route SIEM correlation alerts for data exfiltration, mass export, unauthorised access to claims or medical data and privileged misuse into the incident queue with the personal-data flag pre-set.

Add the non-technical channels: misdirected post and email reported by the contact centre, lost devices and papers reported by the service desk, claims-file disclosure reported by adjusters, and processor notifications.
Publish a single internal reporting route and a one-hour internal reporting expectation for any staff member who suspects a breach, and put it in the annual training.
Review the queue every shift so a report sitting unread cannot delay the awareness timestamp.
checklist.done: every technical and human channel writes into one incident queue that is reviewed each shift.

checklist.step: Triage within one hour and confirm personal-data involvement
actions: Open the case within one hour, classify the incident type - confidentiality, integrity or availability breach - and confirm whether personal data is in scope.
Identify the systems and data stores touched and pull the data classification for each from the catalogue so special-category involvement is known immediately.
Page the Data Protection Officer and Privacy Counsel as soon as personal data is confirmed, using the on-call rota rather than email.
Set the 72-hour countdown on the case and record the awareness timestamp that started it.
checklist.done: each case is triaged within an hour with personal-data scope confirmed, the DPO paged and the 72-hour countdown running.

checklist.step: Contain and preserve evidence without destroying the record
actions: Contain first - isolate the host, revoke the session or token, disable the account, block the egress destination - and record each action with its timestamp and the person who took it.
Preserve volatile evidence and logs before remediation overwrites them, and extend log retention on the affected systems for the duration of the investigation.
Take a forensic image where the incident may lead to litigation or regulatory action, and maintain the chain of custody record.
Never re-image or restore a system before the evidence capture is signed off by the Incident Response Lead.
checklist.done: containment actions are timestamped and attributed, and evidence is preserved with an intact chain of custody before remediation.

checklist.step: Establish the scope: whose data, what data, how much
actions: Quantify the affected records and the distinct data subjects, split by jurisdiction, since EU and UK subjects drive different filings.
List the data categories involved, calling out health and medical evidence, financial account details, identity documents and conviction data separately.
Establish whether the data was encrypted with keys the attacker did not hold, since that determines whether the Art. 34(3)(a) exemption is available.
Where the exact population cannot be fixed inside 72 hours, record the best current estimate and its basis - an estimate is filed, silence is not.
checklist.done: the record states affected subject counts by jurisdiction, data categories, encryption state, and the basis of any estimate.

checklist.step: Assess the risk to rights and freedoms
actions: Score the risk using the EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 factors: type of breach, nature and sensitivity of the data, ease of identification, severity of consequences, special characteristics of the data subjects and of the controller, and the number of individuals affected.

Reason about concrete harms for an insurer - a disclosed health condition affecting employment or relationships, identity theft from an application pack, fraud from claim payment details, distress from a claim history reaching a third party.
Reach one of three conclusions and write the reasoning: not notifiable, notifiable to the authority, or notifiable to the authority and to the individuals.
Record any decision not to notify with the same rigour as a decision to notify, because Art. 33(5) requires it to be verifiable.
checklist.done: a written, factor-by-factor risk assessment reaches a stated notifiability conclusion with reasoning captured.

checklist.step: File the supervisory-authority notification inside 72 hours
actions: Identify the lead supervisory authority - the Irish DPC under the Art. 56 one-stop-shop for cross-border EU processing - and add the ICO where UK data subjects are affected.

Complete the Art. 33(3) content: the nature of the breach including the categories and approximate number of data subjects and of records; the DPO's name and contact details; the likely consequences; and the measures taken or proposed, including mitigation.

Submit through the authority's own route - the Irish DPC breach notification webform and the ICO personal data breach report service - and record the reference number and submission timestamp on the incident record.
Where filing past 72 hours, state the reasons for the delay in the form itself as Art. 33(1) requires, and never backdate the awareness timestamp to make the window fit.
checklist.done: the notification is submitted with an authority reference and timestamp, all Art. 33(3) elements completed, and any delay reasoned in the form.

checklist.step: Supply phased detail as the investigation develops
actions: Where the initial filing used estimates, commit in the form to a follow-up date and meet it under Art. 33(4).
Send updates when the affected population is fixed, when root cause is established and when containment and remediation complete.
Log every authority query and the response given, with the date, on the incident record.
Keep Privacy Counsel on every submission so admissions and characterisations stay consistent across filings.
checklist.done: each phased update is filed against the original reference by its committed date, and all authority correspondence is logged.

checklist.step: Decide the Art. 34 communication to individuals
actions: Apply the Art. 34(1) test: does the breach result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.

Test the three Art. 34(3) exemptions honestly - appropriate technical protection such as encryption rendering the data unintelligible, subsequent measures that ensure the high risk is no longer likely to materialise, or disproportionate effort requiring instead a public communication.
Where an exemption is relied on, write out why it applies to this data and this population, and record that the supervisory authority may still require communication under Art. 34(4).
Sign the decision and file it on the incident record before any communication or non-communication is finalised.
checklist.done: a signed Art. 34 decision exists stating high risk or the specific exemption relied on, with reasoning tied to this population.

checklist.step: Communicate to affected individuals in clear and plain language
actions: Draft the notification with the Art. 34(2) content: the nature of the breach in plain terms, the DPO's contact details, the likely consequences, and the measures taken or proposed including mitigation the individual can take.
Say what data of theirs was involved specifically - a generic 'some personal information' notice fails the clear-and-plain-language test.
Give practical steps: change credentials, watch for phishing referencing their claim, contact the credit reference agencies, and give a dedicated phone line and reference.
Have Privacy Counsel and the Data Protection Officer approve the wording before despatch, and localise it for each jurisdiction and language.
checklist.done: an approved, localised notification stating the specific data involved and practical steps is ready for despatch with a dedicated contact route.

checklist.step: Despatch, staff the response line and prove delivery
actions: Despatch by the channel most likely to reach the individual - email plus letter for policyholders, letter for third-party claimants - and record the despatch date and the delivery evidence per subject.
Brief and script the response line before despatch, with escalation to Privacy Ops for rights requests and to Complaints for expressions of dissatisfaction.
Forecast and staff the call volume against the notified population and track abandonment so the line does not fail on day one.
Track bounce-backs and returned post and re-issue through an alternative channel, recording the second attempt.
checklist.done: every notified subject has a recorded despatch and delivery outcome, and the response line is scripted, staffed and monitored.

checklist.step: Handle processor-reported breaches on the contractual clock
actions: On receipt of a processor notification under Art. 33(2), open a controller incident immediately and set the awareness timestamp to the receipt time.
Demand from the processor the Art. 33(3) content set within the contractual 24 hours, escalating to the vendor's named executive contact where it does not arrive.
Assess whether the controller's own 72-hour clock is at risk and file on estimates rather than wait for the processor to be complete.
Raise a contractual finding against the processor where notification was late, and feed it into the audit-rights exercise and the renewal decision.
checklist.done: every processor notification opens a controller incident on receipt, with content chased on the 24-hour clock and lateness raised contractually.

checklist.step: Maintain the Art. 33(5) internal breach register
actions: Record every personal data breach, including those assessed as not notifiable, with facts, effects and remedial action taken as Art. 33(5) requires.
Include the awareness timestamp, the risk-assessment conclusion and reasoning, the notification decision, the authority reference and the subject-communication decision.
Reconcile the register monthly to the incident queue so any incident flagged as personal data but absent from the register is caught.
Keep the register in a form producible to the supervisory authority to verify compliance, since that is its stated purpose.
checklist.done: every personal data breach, notifiable or not, has a register entry with facts, effects, remedial action and decision reasoning.

checklist.step: Run the post-incident review and close the root cause
actions: Hold the review within 10 working days of containment with the CISO, the DPO and the affected system owner.
Reconstruct the chronology and measure detection-to-awareness and awareness-to-notification in hours, naming what consumed the time.
Agree corrective actions - control changes, monitoring rules, process changes, training - each with an owner and a date, and track them in the GRC platform.
Feed the lessons into the next breach simulation and into the annual privacy training content.
checklist.done: a dated post-incident review exists with the measured chronology, root cause and owned corrective actions in the tracker.

checklist.step: Rehearse the 72-hour path twice a year
actions: Run a half-yearly table-top exercise on a realistic scenario - a claims file share exposed, a mail-house mis-merge, a ransomware event on the underwriting platform - with the real on-call people, not deputies.
Time the exercise against the real clock: awareness declared, DPO engaged, scope estimated, draft Art. 33(3) content produced, notify decision taken.
Include the actual completion of a draft Irish DPC webform and ICO report so the content gaps surface in the exercise rather than in an incident.
Write the exercise report with the measured times and the gaps found, and assign each gap an owner and a date.
checklist.done: a half-yearly exercise report exists with measured timings, a drafted authority form and owned gap actions.

testing.step: Build the population of incidents and breaches
actions: Extract every security and privacy incident raised in the period with type, personal-data flag, detection, report and awareness timestamps and closure date.
Add reports made outside the ticketing system - contact-centre misdirected-mail logs, service-desk lost-device records, complaints citing wrongful disclosure and processor notification emails.
Extract the Art. 33(5) breach register separately, since the register and the queue diverge exactly where the finding is.
Sign both extracts as complete and record run dates and row counts.
testing.done: signed incident-queue and breach-register extracts exist, supplemented by the non-ticketed reporting channels.

testing.step: Reconcile the incident queue to the Art. 33(5) register
actions: Match every personal-data-flagged incident to a register entry and list the unmatched.
Independently review 20 incidents flagged as not involving personal data and test the flag against the systems and data stores actually touched, using the data catalogue classification.
List every complaint or contact-centre record describing a wrongful disclosure with no incident and no register entry.
Treat every unregistered breach as an automatic exception.
testing.done: the queue and register are reconciled both ways and every unregistered or mis-flagged breach is listed.

testing.step: Draw and document the sample
actions: Take 100% of notified breaches, 100% of breaches involving special-category data and 100% of processor-reported breaches.
Take 100% of assessed-not-notifiable breaches involving more than 100 data subjects, since that is where the wrong call is expensive.
Take 20 further incidents at random with a recorded seed from the remaining personal-data population.
Record population size, seed, strata and draw date so the sample is reproducible.
testing.done: a reproducible sample covers all notified, special-category, processor-reported and large not-notified breaches plus a random tail.

testing.step: Re-perform the awareness timestamp from the underlying evidence
actions: For each sampled incident, read the SIEM alert time, the first human report, the triage note and the chat or bridge transcript, and set your own awareness time from the evidence.
Compare it to the recorded awareness timestamp and list every incident where the recorded time is later than the evidence supports.
Compute detection-to-awareness hours and flag anything over 24 hours for root-cause comment.
Treat a late-set awareness timestamp as an exception in its own right, because it manufactures compliance with the 72-hour window.
testing.done: each sampled incident has an independently derived awareness time, with every late-set timestamp listed as an exception.

testing.step: Recompute the 72-hour window against the filing
actions: For each notified breach, compute elapsed hours = authority submission timestamp minus the re-performed awareness timestamp, using calendar hours including weekends.
List every filing over 72 hours and check whether the form itself carries the Art. 33(1) reasons for the delay.
Check that where UK subjects were affected, an ICO report was filed as well as the DPC notification, and compute its window separately.
Recompute the processor cases from the processor-notification receipt time and test the contractual 24-hour clock against the vendor's actual notification.
testing.done: elapsed-hour maths is recomputed for every notified breach and each late filing is listed with its delay reasoning tested.

testing.step: Trace filings to the authority reference and re-read their content
actions: Open the submitted form or its saved copy for each notified breach and confirm the authority reference number and submission timestamp exist on the incident record.
Grid the form content against Art. 33(3)(a)-(d): nature with categories and approximate numbers of subjects and records, DPO contact, likely consequences, and measures taken or proposed.
Compare the numbers stated to the final scope figures and confirm a phased Art. 33(4) update was filed where the initial figures were estimates.
Capture the submitted form and the authority acknowledgement into the workpaper.
testing.done: every filing traces to an authority reference, has a completed Art. 33(3) content grid, and phased updates are evidenced where estimates were filed.

testing.step: Re-perform the risk and Art. 34 decisions
actions: For each sampled breach, apply the EDPB Guidelines 9/2022 factors yourself from the incident facts before reading the recorded assessment.
Compare conclusions; a difference in either direction - unnotified when it should have been, or notified without reasoning - is an exception.

For each Art. 34(3) exemption relied on, test it against the facts: was the data genuinely encrypted with keys the attacker did not hold, did the subsequent measures actually remove the high risk, was the disproportionate-effort claim backed by a public communication.
Confirm the decision was signed and dated by the DPO before the communication or non-communication was finalised.
testing.done: each risk and Art. 34 decision is independently re-performed, with unsupported exemptions and missing sign-offs listed as fails.

testing.step: Trace subject notifications to delivery evidence
actions: For each high-risk breach, reconcile the notified-subject count to the affected-subject count and explain any shortfall.
Sample 20 notified subjects and confirm a despatch record and delivery outcome exists for each, including re-issue where the first attempt bounced or was returned.
Read the notification text against Art. 34(2) - nature, DPO contact, likely consequences, measures and mitigation advice - and against the plain-language standard.
Check the elapsed time from awareness to despatch and comment where it stretched beyond what the facts justify.
testing.done: notified counts reconcile to affected counts, sampled subjects have delivery evidence, and the text meets the Art. 34(2) content test.

testing.step: Log exceptions with root cause, owner and remediation date
actions: Raise one issue per exception naming the incident, the failure (late-set awareness, filing past 72 hours without reasons, unregistered breach, unsupported Art. 34 exemption, no subject notification, processor late) and the subjects affected.
Assign root cause - channel not feeding the queue, triage waiting for forensic certainty, DPO paged late, scope estimate withheld, processor contract clock not enforced - and a named owner.
Set a remediation date and, where a notifiable breach was never filed, ask the Data Protection Officer to decide on a late self-report to the authority.
Carry every open issue into the next quarter's test and into the next breach simulation scenario.
testing.done: every exception has an issue with root cause, owner, remediation date, a late-self-report decision where needed, and a retest commitment.

testing.step: Conclude, obtain independent sign-off and report
actions: Compute the within-72-hour filing rate, the count of late-set awareness timestamps, the register-completeness rate and the high-risk subject-notification rate against the stated thresholds.
Write the conclusion - effective, effective with exceptions, or ineffective - citing the workpaper reference behind each figure, and include the timings measured in the half-yearly simulation.
Have the Internal Auditor, who handled and decided no sampled incident, sign the workpaper as independent reviewer.
Report to the Data Protection Officer, the Chief Info Security Officer and the Board Risk Committee at its next sitting and file the workpaper under REG-020-C06 in the compliance evidence repository.
testing.done: a signed workpaper with a stated conclusion, the four computed measures, simulation timings and a dated committee reporting entry is filed.

Accountable obligation owner.value: Privacy Office owns curriculum content and the role-based training matrix under the DPO's Art. 39(1)(b) awareness-raising duty; Learning & Development owns delivery, assignment and completion chasing through the LMS

Citation verified against current regula.value: Yes - GDPR Art. 39(1)(b) DPO duty of awareness-raising and training of staff involved in processing, Art. 32(4) and Art. 29 requiring persons acting under the controller's authority to process only on instruction, Art. 5(2) accountability for demonstrating it, and Art. 33 for the 72-hour breach reporting content the workforce must trigger; UK content checked against ICO accountability framework training expectations

In-scope processes.value: Annual mandatory privacy training for all EU and UK staff and contractors, plus role-specific modules for underwriters and medical underwriting, claims handlers and adjusters, SIU investigators, contact-centre agents, marketing, HR, and developers and data scientists handling production data; new-joiner training and post-incident targeted training

In-scope systems.value: Curriculum, assignment, completion and assessment scores held in the LMS, driven off the HRIS worker and contractor feed; role-based assignment rules keyed to job profile and org unit; attestations and evidence exported to the compliance evidence repository

Compliance procedure documented.value: Privacy Training Procedure - annual curriculum refresh, role-based matrix and assignment rules, new-joiner completion inside 30 days of start date, pass mark and re-sit rules, non-completion escalation ladder, and targeted retraining triggered by breach root causes and DSAR failures

Compliance procedure approved.value: Approved by the Data Protection Officer and the Chief HR Officer; curriculum content re-approved annually before the campaign opens and after any notifiable breach whose root cause was human

Filing/reporting deadlines tracked.value: Annual campaign opens 1 March and closes 30 April for all existing staff; new joiners and transfers into an in-scope role complete within 30 days of start or transfer date; targeted retraining after an incident completes within 30 days of the post-incident review

Deadline reminders configured.value: LMS reminders at day 14, day 21 and day 27 of the new-joiner 30-day window; campaign reminders at two weeks and one week before close, then weekly line-manager escalation lists; a daily overdue report to HR Business Partners after close

Violations/exceptions logged with dispos.value: Non-completion past the campaign close or the 30-day new-joiner window, role-based modules not assigned to an in-scope population, and failure to complete post-incident retraining are logged with the individual, the line manager and a remediation date

Remediation sign-off captured.value: The DPO signs the annual curriculum, the completion conclusion at campaign close, and the remediation plan for any population left untrained or assigned the wrong module

Test population (in-scope transactions,.value: All active EU and UK workers and contractors on the HRIS at campaign close, all joiners and role-transfers in the period, and all individuals named in incident root causes or DSAR failures requiring targeted retraining

Pass/fail thresholds.value: At least 98% completion of the annual module by campaign close and 100% for staff handling special-category data; 100% of new joiners complete within 30 days; assessment pass mark 80% with a maximum of two re-sits; any in-scope population with no assigned role module is an automatic fail

Compliance test frequency matched to the.value: The obligation is annual, so the completeness test runs at campaign close over the full workforce, with a quarterly test of new-joiner 30-day compliance and a post-incident test whenever targeted retraining is triggered
